Breaking.title: Andy Burnham promises to 'move quickly' on Neets report
Breaking.text:
The prime minister has said he wants to "move quickly" on implementing recommendations in Alan Milburn's report on work and young people.

Speaking to BBC Breakfast, Andy Burnham said: "This isn't about waiting forever and a long-off-promised reform, I want to get stuck into it right now."

Milburn's report, external urged more job support for under-25s, a shake-up of the benefits system, early intervention in schools and tax cuts for businesses hiring young people.

The government said it backed the review's principles and is expected to set out which proposals it will take on shortly.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said there was no need for "costly government schemes to fix Labour's own mistakes".

"We need to stop making it so expensive and risky to hire young people," she added.

Last year, the government asked Milburn, a former Labour minister, to do a review into the rising number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet), which has now reached almost one million.

Burnham praised the report as a "landmark moment" adding: "This is not just a benefits reform, it's a whole society change he is calling for."

Asked what the number of young people not in education, employment or training should be by the next election, Burnham said he wanted the level to come down "as soon as possible".

He said he wanted 45-day work placements offered to every 16-18-year-old "who wants one" and was working on funding the places.

The government has also announced it will fully fund college places for everyone aged 16 to 18 in England for 2027/28.

The Association of Colleges said the money would allow its members to enrol thousands of extra students each year "confident in the knowledge that they will receive funding for them".

Burnham said he wanted to get the benefit bill down adding: "No one can be comfortable with the idea of hundreds of thousands of young people on benefits - nobody, not me, not anyone."

However, he added that it required "more than the crude cuts the other parties are offering".

"All of my experience says a 'names not numbers' approach that looks at the whole person, their housing, their debt, their mental health issues and creates a rounded response, that is proven to be more successful at getting people into work."

In his report, Milburn warned that employer National Insurance, wage costs, business rates and employment protections could be factors in deterring employers from hiring unexperienced young people.

"Fair pay, greater security and predictable hours matter," Milburn said, but added that the cost and complexity of hiring young people had increased "sharply".

On workers' rights, Burnham argued a balance had to be struck adding: "The more you strengthen employment security that creates more durable jobs that young people are more likely to stay in."

Asked if former Chancellor Rachel Reeves had made the situation worse by increasing the tax employers pay, the prime minister said the government had increased support for those hiring long-term unemployed people.

He also defended his reset with the EU, which could make it easier for young Europeans to work in the UK.

He argued that a closer relationship with the EU would help grow the economy, which would provide more opportunities for young people.

Attempts to change the welfare system under Sir Keir Starmer last year failed when Labour backbenchers refused to support the £5bn cuts to benefits, raising concerns about the impact on disabled people.

So far, there are few signs that Burnham's plans will trigger a similar backlash, although some Labour backbenchers and the Unison trade union have said the proposals on benefits could push young people into poverty.

Steve Darling, the Liberal Democrat work and pensions spokesman, said the government should "scrap the damaging job tax" and work with European countries to grow the economy.

Green Party MP Sian Berry urged the minister to "reject cuts" for young disabled people.

"One million young people need a leg up - one that does not come with the chair being kicked out from under them," she said.

Reform UK said immigration was the "elephant in the room" and called on the government to cut employer national insurance for British workers "so that young Brits are at the front of the queue for new jobs".

Breaking.title: Chris Mason: Milburn may have gifted Labour MPs a moral argument for welfare reform
Breaking.text:
The prime minister describes Alan Milburn's report on jobs, training and benefits for young people as a "watershed moment".

In so doing, he is accepting Milburn's case for change and taking on the task of delivering it. Were ministers to actually manage that, it would amount to one of the most significant shake-ups of the welfare state in its history.

But the proposed timeframe for this stretches to a decade, which is another geological era in political terms, at least two general elections away.

Milburn is a deft operator. From a round of morning television and radio interviews, to addressing the cabinet, to releasing his report into the wild, he was still out and about on Tuesday evening in Westminster persuading, charming and cajoling those possibly in need of all three.

And this former MP, still every inch the politician, has an ongoing role - appointed the chairman of the government's new Youth Opportunities Unit.

The new job, which will report directly to Andy Burnham, is about tying together the myriad different aspects of change he is suggesting, involving multiple government departments.

And yes, it does mean a 68-year-old bloke becomes an early beneficiary of new employment prospects for the young.

But that glib observation apart, there is a hope that Milburn has gifted Labour MPs a moral argument for welfare reforms they can endorse. Or, to put it more bluntly, one not grounded in a specific objective to make benefits cuts to make the sums add up elsewhere.

Plus, him hanging around perhaps means he can be a useful lightning conductor for any forthcoming angst on Labour's benches – as having persuaded them of the big picture mission, the gritty reality of implementing it begins to take shape.

As the prime minister puts it in an interview in the Times, external, the government wants to offer "a new social contract" for "the let-down generation".

And he tells the newspaper that the initial upfront cost of around £500m, for employment support in 2027-28, will come from existing government budgets, which will mean cuts to other things elsewhere in government.

"I've asked the cabinet to reprioritise," he said.

Crucially, if you are in Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland, many of the decisions around whether or not to press ahead with these ideas will be up to the devolved governments in Edinburgh, Cardiff and Belfast.

From the government at Westminster's perspective, the focus now will be drawing up the specific plans for implementing Milburn's ideas, having accepted the broad thrust of his argument.

A white paper will follow in the new year, and then legislation.

What we don't know yet and will be crucial to the next stage of this debate, is precisely who will be the perceived winners and losers, at least in the short term, of the proposed changes.

Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden told me that "those with the most severe and lifelong disabilities where work is not a realistic prospect" should, as Milburn suggests, "get more support than they receive at the moment". But how will those in this category be defined?

McFadden also told me that for some of those facing "extra costs" associated with their circumstances "there will be an extra cost benefit that will make at least a contribution towards that".

Again, how will those in this category be defined?

There is too an emerging political argument, following remarks from Alan Milburn already seized upon by the Conservatives, that decisions taken by Labour in its first few years in power have made a difficult situation harder still for young people looking for work.

On page 66 of his report, external, Milburn says the Employment Rights Act 2025 "could have major implications at a time when the youth labour market is already weak".

Interestingly, on this point, the prime minister is willing to push back, telling BBC Breakfast that "there is a balance to be struck".

"It is important to consider on the other side of this that the more you strengthen employment security, that can create more durable jobs that young people are more likely to stay in," he says. "We're going to consider all of this in the round."

The big decisions, then, now sit on the prime minister and the work and pensions secretary's desks.

In accepting the magnitude of Milburn's diagnosis and proposed treatment, they are tacitly accepting too that it is their responsibility to deliver – or at least begin to deliver – on much of what he suggests.

Their success or otherwise will matter to this generation of young people and those that will follow – and to the sustainability of the benefits system in the years ahead.

Breaking.title: Waymo temporarily pulls driverless taxis from all US freeways
Breaking.text:
Waymo has temporarily suspended its driverless vehicles from operating on all US freeways, the company has said.

The decision comes after California banned Waymo's driverless taxis from state freeways following a series of recent traffic incidents.

California's Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) cited an "imminent hazard to public safety" for the ban, noting an incident this month in which several driverless Waymo vehicles entered an active construction zone on US Route 101.

Waymo said it was working with state officials "diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations", adding that no injuries or collisions were reported following the incident on US Route 101 south of San Francisco.

California's DMV said Waymo's driverless taxis presented a risk "due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present".

In another incident earlier this month, footage widely seen on social media appeared to show a Waymo car trying to overtake patrol vehicles that were deliberately slowing the pace of traffic on a San Francisco highway.

The California ban, which came into effect on 11 November, would remain in place until Waymo "demonstrates to the department that it has taken effective corrective actions to address the deficiencies that precipitated the restrictions".

A Waymo spokesperson said: "In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance."

Data on Waymo's website suggests that its cars, compared to human drivers, are involved in 95% fewer crashes resulting in serious injury.

Waymo currently operates driverless taxis in 15 US cities, but only offered freeway rides in a handful of those locations, including San Francisco, Los Angeles and Miami.

The company's driverless taxis can continue to operate on regular city streets.

In May, Waymo recalled thousands of its self-driving cars in the US over a software issue that could allow vehicles to drive into flooded roads.

Breaking.title: Irishman charged with destroying US military aircraft with axe
Breaking.text:
US officials have charged an Irishman with destroying a $60m (£45m) American military aircraft after he allegedly snuck onto the tarmac of an airport in Ireland.

Daithi O'Corrain, 48, is accused of doing extensive research before he allegedly used chemicals and various tools - including an axe - to damage a US Air National Guard C-130 Hercules parked at Shannon Airport near Limerick.

American prosecutors have charged him with destruction of government property, which carries a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison.

O'Corrain is not currently in US custody, according to the Associated Press news agency, and it is unclear whether he has a lawyer who could speak on his behalf.

In filings unsealed by prosecutors in New York on Tuesday, agents from the FBI argued that the act jeopardised US national security. They say the plane was parked at the airport while en route to another country on a US military assignment.

"As alleged, Daithi O'Corrain carried out a deliberate, planned attack against a US military aircraft, causing tens of millions of dollars in damage and jeopardizing critical military operations," prosecutors said in a court filing.

"This was not an act of spontaneous vandalism," said FBI Assistant Director in Charge James Barnacle Jr, explaining O'Corrain "spent months researching the aircraft, acquiring tools and materials, and preparing to maximize the destruction he could inflict."

Officials say that the suspect planned extensively for the 11 April 2026 raid, and brought tools with him for the demolition, which took place over several hours.

He entered the plane by breaking a locking mechanism, officials say, then used straps to close the doors before covering the windows.

"O'Corrain then proceeded to inflict severe damage to the interior of the Aircraft by, among other things, cutting wire bundles and hydraulic lines within the Aircraft, crimping a liquid oxygen line within the Aircraft, destroying every gauge in the Aircraft's cockpit, and puncturing the Aircraft's air ducts," the US indictment says.

He also used gallium, a substance that can erode aluminum and steel, ball bearings which he poured in the fuel tank, and an axe which he used to puncture the exterior of the plane.

He was caught by airport crew, and filmed standing on top of the plane. He was arrested at the scene, and charged by Ireland's national police with causing criminal damages.

Breaking.title: American soldier arrested in UK taken into US military custody
Breaking.text:
A US Army officer arrested in the UK on suspicion of spying for Russia earlier this month has been taken into US military custody, British counter-terror police havesaid.

The serviceman has been identified as Lt Col Brandon Carroll Tyner, BBC News understands. The 41-year-old - who served in the US Army since 2008 - was arrested near Gloucester last week by British counter-terror police.

Tyner was based at Imjin Barracks in Innsworth, Gloucestershire, the headquarters of Nato's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps.

Counter Terrorism Policing said he is now in US custody over suspected national security and espionage allegations. At the time of his arrest, Russia said it had "nothing to do with it".

British police previously said he was being held in London after he was arrested under section one and section three of the National Security Act 2023, which relate to obtaining or disclosing protected information, and assisting a foreign intelligence service.

The day after Tyner's arrest on 10 November, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he was "unaware" of what it was connected to.

"We have nothing to do with it, and it has nothing to do with us," he told reporters in Moscow.

On Tuesday, Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing, said: "Subsequently, a decision was made to pass the investigation to them [their American partners] to progress."

"These are extremely serious allegations, and our collective response should send a strong message that we will act swiftly and robustly where we suspect this kind of espionage activity taking place," he added.

Tyner's arrest was the result of a long-running operation by MI5 - the UK's domestic intelligence and security agency - in collaboration with the FBI, the BBC understands.

He had previously served in Afghanistan and Iraq, but at the time of his arrest was working with NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps near Gloucester - where he was said to be entrusted with sensitive information which would have been extremely damaging if leaked to Russia.

Detectives sent the Crown Prosecution Service a file on the senior US soldier's alleged spying for consideration - allegations described by the head of Counter Terrorism Policing as "extremely serious."

But at that stage the Attorney General's Office in London got involved. As did the US authorities.

And now the decision has been taken that Lieutenant Colonel Tyner should be taken into custody by the US Military.

It means he will not stand trial in the UK, but under US Uniform Code of Military Justice.

Breaking.title: Philippines police ask prosecutors to charge Thomas Markle over child sex abuse material
Breaking.text:
Police in the Philippines have asked prosecutors to charge Thomas Markle Sr, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, with possession of and intent to distribute child sexual abuse material.

Cebu province prosecutor Graeme Elmido told the BBC that police had filed documents requesting that Markle be charged on Monday.

Earlier this month, Markle, 82, was separately arrested and charged in the US with possession of child sexual abuse material. The FBI said agents seized about 78 items, including film negatives, slides and books that they allege contained child sex abuse material, from storage units Markle rented.

Markle, who is in custody in the US, has previously denied the allegations. The BBC has contacted Markle's attorney for comment.

Elmido told the BBC that Philippine National Police had asked prosecutors to charge Markle with "two counts of intent to distribute CSAEM [child sexual abuse and exploitation material], and one count of possession of CSAEM material".

Last month, police in the Philippines obtained a warrant to examine devices allegedly removed from Markle's former home in the country.

Four boxes of material, including computers, phones, hard drives and old video tapes, were handed to officers by Meghan's half brother Thomas Markle Jr.

Earlier this month, Markle Sr was arrested and charged in the US. He had initially been placed under house detention at his assisted living facility in Florida, but was taken back into custody last week after prosecutors alleged he removed his ankle monitor.

Meghan Markle has been estranged from her father since 2018. The BBC understands she broke contact with him last year, telling him she and the authorities knew he had abused young girls.

In a previously shared statement after the allegations against her father emerged, Meghan wrote: "I am deeply distressed... my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed."

She said she hoped it could be understood why she had largely cut off contact from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children".

Breaking.title: Home secretary plans to tackle 'perception of two-tier policing'
Breaking.text:
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood is to announce stronger guidance on police impartiality to tackle what she calls the "corrosive and growing perception of two-tier policing".

She will tell a conference of police chiefs that they should avoid what she calls "misguided attempts at course correction" where the pursuit of equality leads instead to differential treatment.

Recent complaints about alleged two-tier policing have mostly come from those on the right in politics.

They have pointed to the arrest of Henry Nowak as he was dying after being stabbed by Vickrum Digwa who had accused him of racism.

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has argued that white people are treated differently by police because of their race. But critics say this claim risks overlooking the long‑standing experiences of black and minority ethnic communities.

Some senior police figures have also strongly rejected the claim of two-tier policing.

Mahmood will announce a new national standard is being developed "to ensure all members of the public are treated equally", said the Home Office.

"Now let me be clear: I know the vast majority of officers police impartially and that policing without fear or favour is their creed," she will say.

But Mahmood will announce "clear, comprehensive guidance" on police impartiality, which reinforces that officers must apply the law consistently to avoid what she called "motivated actors" whipping up the idea that there's two-tier policing.

Mahmood will say that community engagement can mean going to a residents' association meeting and having tea and biscuits - or samosas - but it shouldn't mean engaging with activists pushing an agenda.

"Leave the politics to the politicians," she will say. "And we will leave the policing to you."

The home secretary will add that more needs to be done to tackle inequalities in policing, highlighting the persistently low proportion of black police officers.

However, she will state that some "well-intentioned approaches", such as the Police Anti-Racism Commitment, "have risked undermining confidence in impartial policing".

"As a Muslim home secretary, no one can doubt that equality in policing, and in our forces, matters to me," she will say.

"But we must also be wary of misguided attempts at course correction, where the pursuit of equality leads instead to differential treatment.

"To the public, it was patently absurd to tell police officers that fair policing "does not mean treating everyone the same".

Jo Noakes who leads the College of Policing, the standards-setting body for the police, said it will issue new guidance for officers that will make clear on impartiality in Spring.

She said: "Policing must act in a way that maintains public confidence, which is dependent on officers and staff exercising their powers without fear or favour...

"Impartiality cannot be seen in isolation but needs to be considered alongside how policing acts with fairness and inclusion - both in its own ranks and with the public."

Breaking.title: Cutting EV target risks UK missing climate targets, warns adviser
Breaking.text:
The UK is likely to miss legally binding climate targets if the government reduces electric vehicle (EV) targets, independent adviser the Climate Change Committee (CCC) has warned.

In a letter to Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander, the CCC argues that weakening the targets would result in "economic and energy security costs" and leave households "more exposed to volatile fossil fuel prices".

The CCC says that switching to an electric vehicle can save a typical household around £800 a year, with fewer people benefiting if the targets were watered down.

The warning comes after weeks of speculation that the government plans to announce changes to the EV targets. Government sources insist no decision has been made.

Under the current rules, a "zero emission vehicle" (ZEV) mandate requires 80% of new cars sold in the UK to be zero emission by 2030 and all new cars to meet that standard by 2035. Companies that fail to meet their ZEV mandate face a potential fine of £12,000 per car, although there are exemptions.

Industry groups have long complained the current rules impose too heavy a burden, calling instead for a "sustainable transition".

Latest data from trade body the Society of Motor Manufacturing and Traders (SMMT) shows that EVs, as well as plug-in hybrids, are driving growth in new car sales.

In the year so far, 26.6% of all new car registrations have been fully electric, the SMMT says, which is below the headline target of 33% for 2026.

But the industry as a whole appears on course to comply with this year's mandate once flexibilities are accounted for, according to analysis by New AutoMotive, a transport research organisation which supports the transition to electric cars

SMMT Chief Executive Mike Hawes accused the CCC of ignoring the costs of the targets it was defending.

"The industry cannot subsidise the transition indefinitely, which is why it is unified in seeking change," he said.

Breaking.title: Putin's Crimean Bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine
Breaking.text:
Ukraine has severely damaged a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, in what President Volodymyr Zelensky says was an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.

Images shared by Ukrainian officials show a section of the Crimean Bridge collapsed into the water, dealing a logistical and symbolic blow to Moscow's war effort.

The Kremlin said it would rebuild the bridge "better than before".

Meanwhile in Kyiv, Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said traffic had partially resumed on the Pivnichnyi (Northern) and Pivdennyi (Southern) bridges - key crossings over the Dnipro River - after they had been closed following Russian strikes overnight.

Ukraine has long targeted the Crimean Bridge, which provides a road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line, but has struggled to close it for good.

While Kyiv has been trying to increase the cost to Russia of waging war economically, by hitting oil refineries and depots, striking the bridge is an attempt to increase the political cost on Russian President Vladimir Putin.

The timing of the strike comes at a significant moment, ahead of Putin meeting the leaders of China and the US. This could cloud his moment back in the spotlight.

The Crimean Bridge was built by Russia after it invaded and illegally annexed Ukraine's southern peninsula in 2014.

The $3.6bn (£2.7bn) piece of infrastructure is widely seen in Russia and Ukraine as Putin's personal pet project: His close tycoon friend Arkady Rotenberg built it, and then Putin personally opened it by driving a lorry over it in May 2018.

In Ukraine, the much-hated bridge is seen as one of the main symbols of Russia's continuing occupation of Ukrainian lands.

"We're drinking champagne!" Andrii, an engineer who lives in Kyiv, told the BBC.

He said the latest attack would "deal a very heavy blow to the morale of the Russians".

Some Ukrainians are concerned that Putin might now respond by carrying out even more attacks against civilian infrastructure, but Andrii said: "I don't think the Russians can make things much worse; they're already pounding us every single night with everything they've got."

The damage after the overnight attack, involving cruise missiles and drones, appeared to be far more severe than during previous strikes on the bridge, with a large arched section apparently destroyed.

Video footage appeared to show critical damage to the road section, with remnants of the support arch and road deck seen protruding from the water below.

Zelensky said the strike was the result of a seven-stage operation by the military and security services, which saw Ukrainian forces "gradually destroy air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment, and other designated targets on the way to the final objective".

He said several types of Ukrainian drones as well as the country's Flamingo and Neptune cruise missiles were fired overnight during a "pivotal stage".

The Ukrainian president also said the rail section parallel to the bridge's road had also been hit by a wave of drones, though images showed its supporting arch was still standing and Russia's transport ministry later said some rail services resumed.

Ukraine's state security service SBU said its operations had "systematically suppressed enemy air defence systems" over a month, and said it showed "no Russian defence systems can guarantee the safety of illegal objects occupied by the invaders".

Meanwhile, Ukraine's military said the roadway on the bridge is "out of action", with no vehicle able to cross it, and the railway section is still standing, but with a damaged arch.

The Kremlin said Putin had been briefed on the overnight attack. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the bridge would "be restored following Ukrainian strikes, and it will be even better than before", and did not rule out the possibility the strikes were linked to Putin's visit to China.

Russia's Investigative Committee confirmed structural damage and said it had opened a "criminal case... on terrorism charges" after attacks by "Ukraine's armed formations".

For the second day in a row, Russia recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, with 2,256 drones downed, according to the defence ministry.

Zelensky had warned of major attacks in the days leading up to a meeting between Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in China's Shenzhen on Thursday.

The long-term impact of the Crimean Bridge strike is still not fully clear, though the risk of a serious transport and logistics crisis for the Russian military has increased significantly.

The collapse of the arched section has cut off the peninsula's direct road and rail links with Russia – at least until the crossing can be repaired.

However, there is still a land corridor running through the occupied parts of Ukraine's southern Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions - though Kyiv has been systematically striking transport routes across northern Crimea, as well as bridges and other crossings in the area around Chongar.

This has already caused problems with the delivery of fuel and other supplies, including military cargo.

There is a ferry crossing across the Kerch Strait, which connects the Black Sea with the Sea of Azov. It could partly compensate for the loss of the bridge, but its capacity is very limited and it is also vulnerable to attack.

Russia could also supply Crimea by sea, but this route is also risky, as Ukrainian naval and aerial drones operate extensively in the area.

In addition, debris from the Crimean Bridge – particularly its enormous arch – may have blocked the shipping channel.

This would make it harder for larger vessels to pass through and create further problems for the Russian-occupied ports in the Sea of Azov, including Mariupol and Berdyansk.

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine is now under Russian occupation and Kyiv has refused Putin's demand to give up areas of Ukraine's eastern Donbas that remain under its control.

Breaking.title: How the attack on Putin's prized Crimean Bridge unfolded
Breaking.text:
Stretching across the Kerch Strait in the Black Sea, the Crimean Bridge was always a symbol: for Russia, a prestige project cementing its claim to sovereign Ukrainian territory, and for Ukraine, a hated piece of infrastructure emblematic of Moscow's occupation of the Crimean Peninsula.

A key section of the double-arched, 12-mile-long bridge now lies on the seabed, brought down by an arsenal of Ukrainian long-range weaponry in a seven-stage operation culminating in a dramatic collapse.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said that the bridge "will be rebuilt, and it will be even better than before".

But eight years after its unveiling, the bridge has now become material proof of Kyiv's ability to pierce through Moscow's military defences to hit even its most treasured and protected structures.

The attack on the strategic Crimean Bridge was carried out gradually to cut across several layers of defence, Kyiv confirmed on Tuesday.

For several weeks Ukraine's Security Service and its General Staff gradually destroyed air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare assets, and other designated targets, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.

A significant strike had already been reported on 16 November, when drones hit the bridge at night. Traffic was paused briefly then reinstated, and although the arch over the road section was visibly damaged, the structure remained standing.

But that hit turned out to have been only the penultimate stage of a complex attack.

In the early hours of 17 November, the final strikes dealt a fatal blow to the weakened arch structure.

One verified video - filmed from a camera on board a Ukrainian-made Flamingo missile - shows the weapon approaching the main span of the bridge and heading towards the steel arches, with the footage freezing just before impact.

The Flamingo had potentially been modified to be controlled remotely, which improved its accuracy enough to strike the bridge supports, munitions expert Justin Bronk, from the Royal United Services Institute said.

The missile's "very heavy warhead" made it "more suitable" for attacking the bridge's reinforced concrete spans and supports, Bronk added.

Zelensky later confirmed that several types of missiles and drones had been employed in the attack, which led the massive road arch - weighing thousands of tonnes and measuring about 227m in length - to collapse into the strait.

Daylight images taken from the shores of Crimea to the north show a section about 200m (660ft) long of the tarmac was too dragged below into the sea.

This is clearly critical damage to the crossing. Far from just being a decorative feature of the bridge, the arch played a structural role, transferring loads and supporting the span and helping to ensure the stability of the entire structure.

The parallel arch supporting the railway section has remained standing, although it may also have been damaged. All traffic on the bridge was initially suspended, though trains were later allowed to resume running.

But the damage to the bridge's main span is "catastrophic", Colin Capriani, a structural engineer from Monash University in Melbourne, Australia, told BBC Verify. It was "very hard to envisage" how the bridge could be rebuilt given it is clearly well within range of Ukrainian weaponry, Capriani added.

Major attacks in 2022 and 2023 had already caused serious damage to the road spans of the bridge, but the structure survived.

The difference this time is "the most critical and vulnerable part of the bridge has been hit", said David MacKenzie of engineering consultancy COWI, adding that "although the wreckage of the bridge can be cleared fairly quickly, reinstating full road traffic will take over a year".

Moscow uses Crimea as a military base, with airbases, troop concentrations, training grounds and artillery stockpiles. From there it also carries out strikes on the rest of the country and resupplies its troops in southern Ukraine.

The attack comes after a summer of frequent strikes on Crimea, dictated by Ukraine's stated goal of cutting the peninsula off from Russia. At the time, Kyiv vowed to turn the Crimean Peninsula "into an island".

Now - although it is too early to speak of a complete blockade of Crimea – the risk of a serious transport and logistics crisis has increased significantly.

There is still a land corridor running through the occupied parts of the Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions. However, Ukraine has been systematically striking transport routes across northern Crimea, as well as bridges and other crossings in the area around Chongar, which has already caused problems with the delivery of fuel and other supplies, including military cargo.

Moscow can also still utilise the ferry crossing across the Kerch Strait. It could partly compensate for the loss of the bridge, but its capacity is very limited - and anything on the Black Sea has become vulnerable to attack. Resupplying Crimea by sea is risky, as Ukrainian naval and aerial drones operate extensively in the area.

In addition, debris from the Crimean Bridge - particularly its enormous arch - may have blocked the shipping channel. This would make it harder for larger vessels to pass through and create further problems for ports in the Sea of Azov, including the occupied cities of Mariupol and Berdyansk.

Away from the operational value of the damage to the bridge, the symbolic significance remains.

In 2018, Putin triumphantly drove over the bridge representing the unification of Russia and Crimea in a Russian-made truck. That section of the road now lies on the seabed.

Nearly five years since he launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Putin continues to wreak destruction on Ukraine's civilian population, but his most prized symbols of power are increasingly threatened by Kyiv's reach.

Breaking.title: 'It was really scary': Mother describes sheltering during Russia strikes on Kyiv bridge
Breaking.text:
The alarms warning of a ballistic missile threat went off just before 23:30 on Monday in Kyiv. Moments later came the boom of explosions.

Once again, the main bridges over the broad River Dnipro that cuts through the city were the target and this time the Russian missiles hit what they wanted.

Close to one end of the Pivnichnyi (Northern) bridge there is a large crater and in the pouring rain, water now rushes through it to the river below. Chunks of tarmac and metal are scattered around.

At its broadest point, the jagged hole is about eight metres wide.

The crossing is closed to all traffic apart from the occasional fire engine or police car passing at high speed. By contrast, nearby roads are jammed with cars and trucks, forced to take long detours.

Anyone in a hurry to move around this city has to walk, or cycle, across the bridge, picking their way through the wreckage. In the miserable weather, that also means getting very wet.

Masha and her family moved to a flat next to the bridge because they had been living by a power plant that kept getting hit by Russian missiles.

Last night, she was in the kitchen of their new place when the Russians struck the bridge. She thought her windows would be blown out of their frames by the explosions.

"It was really scary. We had no idea they'd hit here so much. It's like we're cursed," Masha told me, describing grabbing her child and running into the corridor for protection.

But somehow, she still managed to sound cheerful.

"It's difficult, but we're used to it. And we try to take the positive from everything. Like: we survived today! So we can be happy about that."

From the damage, it looks like Russia targeted the same spot on the bridge with a volley of three missiles, aiming to keep the road closed for as long as possible.

A major recovery operation is under way, with firefighters and engineers in fluorescent overalls working to evaluate the extent of the damage. But it looks like the disruption will continue for some time.

Further along the Dnipro River, the Pivdennyi (Southern) bridge was also hit on Monday night, with four missiles.

The metro line across it was suspended for a while, although by mid-afternoon it had been restored. The mayor, Vitali Klitschko, said road transport in one direction was also being partially restored.

On the Pivnichnyi bridge, a man with a bag of tennis rackets on his back was gazing at the crater in front of him. He was heading home from the courts after he had travelled on foot to the left bank.

"It is upsetting," Anatolii told us. "Then when you read the news of what our side did to the Crimea bridge, you do feel a bit better."

Breaking.title: Russian military plane crashes in Siberia killing all 19 on board
Breaking.text:
A Russian military transport plane has crashed in Siberia, killing all 19 people on board, the country's defence ministry said, according to state-run media.

The An-12 aircraft went down during a "scheduled flight" in an "uninhabited area" in the Kemerovo region, the ministry said in a statement.

The ministry added that it preliminarily believed a technical malfunction was the cause of Tuesday's crash. An investigation by Russia's aviation authorities is now under way.

Local Governor Ilya Seredyuk said an emergency response team "quickly extinguished a blaze" after the crash near the village of Yagunovo, and the area was sealed off by police.

Seredyuk, who visited the crash site, said "a helicopter and medical facilities have been put on standby".

The governor added that the "main task" now was to help investigators carry out their work.

He also posted a video showing firefighters combing through what looked like the crash debris, with a number of ambulances also seen standing nearby.

CCTV footage posted on social media appeared to show the moment the plane crashed, with a lighted object falling through the sky in the distance. An explosion then lit up the sky, but the crash was too far away to be seen.

The BBC and Reuters news agency verified the time and date of the footage, while Reuters also verified the location based on features of the scenery that matched satellite imagery of the area.

It was not immediately known whether the crashed aircraft had any cargo on board.

An-12 planes are widely used by the Russian military to transport weaponry and personnel, and also for search and rescue operations.

Business.title: The EU that Burnham is eyeing up is very different to the one Britain left
Business.text:
"Opening the door to uncontrolled immigration," is how Reform UK described it. "Dragging us into the European Union via the back door," was the charge levelled by the Conservatives.

You could be forgiven for expecting drastic change come Friday's EU-UK summit in Brussels judging by some of the criticism levelled by opponents of the Labour government.

Instead, what's on the table is a limited youth work and mobility scheme (the source of Reform's ire), agreement on cross-channel carbon emissions pricing and a deal to ease food trade.

There's also talk of reducing tuition fees for EU students at British universities (something EU member states, like Germany, really want) in exchange for the UK being admitted to an EU manufacturing scheme (which is important to the Burnham government).

Even in these limited areas, I'm told, not all details will be ironed out by the time of Thursday's meeting.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham admitted last week this is all a "step" towards a closer working relationship with Europe.

It's certainly not a leap, and definitely not a matter of rejoining the bloc at this stage.

Other "steps" under immediate discussion are the UK rejoining the EU's electricity market, and the UK trying again to join an EU-backed defence loan scheme.

"Small steps… to make both sides stronger," is how the EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas describes this process. She also warns: "We have in Europe a lot of trauma from Britain leaving [the EU], so things will not be easy."

Bigger, potentially more politically explosive EU-UK questions look likely to follow after Friday's summit. It's thought Burnham may propose rejoining the EU's customs union and/or the single market. There are suggestions he could eventually table a new referendum on rejoining the EU. None of this before the next general election, though.

On this side of the Channel, the debate is very much focused on what Britain might want. Burnham's plan is bold, belated or completely barmy - depending on your political perspective. But there's been little discussion about the EU point of view, and less still on how the EU has changed since Britain left it.

Just how different is the EU in 2026 from the bloc Britain turned its back on a decade ago? And with the UK still mired in arguments over its relationship with Europe, does the EU even want GB back in the fold or would Brussels now rather avoid more drama?

Since 2016, a series of international shocks have fundamentally changed the EU.

The Covid crisis collapsed international supply chains. Europe became aware just how dependent it was on China for medical supplies, for example. Then, Russia's 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine showed the EU how utterly reliant many members were on energy supplies from Moscow. Big EU beasts like Germany and Italy were particularly affected.

The Ukraine war, the continent's biggest active conflict since World War Two, has persuaded the EU that Europe's domestic defence industry and industrial policy needs a boost and far better coordination.

Donald Trump's two stints as US president convinced the EU that it can never again fully rely on the US to be Europe's best friend abroad, either in trade or security terms. And China's attempt to 'dump' cheap cars and steel in Europe, hurting the Continent's businesses, has made the EU more protectionist-minded.

Brussels's main takeaways: Europe should become more self-reliant. And where imports are needed - with fossil fuels, for example - it must diversify which countries it buys from.

The French used to be a lone voice amongst big EU countries, pushing for more protectionism. Other member states prioritised finding the lowest possible prices, as was once the case with Russian gas, for example. Now there's a growing acceptance that economic efficiency must at times be sacrificed to achieve security of supply.

Some think the UK won't want to align itself with an increasingly protectionist, borrow-happy bloc. While an EU member, the free-trade-minded UK was credited with pushing Brussels to be more "British" and make its single market more competitive.

Others point out that Britain has also changed since 2016.

"The British are less 'British' than they once were," Charles Grant, director of the Centre for European Reform, told me. When the EU introduced steel tariffs to protect itself against Chinese dumping, the UK followed suit with its own, similar tariffs. Now, the EU is placing high tariffs on Chinese imports of electric vehicles - and once again the UK is considering a similar move. "Everyone is a bit more French now," says Grant.

Another big EU change, according to European policy expert Georgina Wright, is that EU citizens have become more comfortable with the idea of centralised European power: a pooling of sovereignty in times of emergency.

The Covid crisis prompted the EU to embrace 'common borrowing', where Brussels raises debt on behalf of member states, who then share the benefits and the risks. It was a historic move, particularly for Germany which was once allergic to the idea. Now there's discussion about a new round of common borrowing focused on defence, in answer to Russian aggression and a US proposing to withdraw defence capabilities from Europe.

Some in the EU tell me that none of this would be possible had the more sovereign-minded UK remained a member state.

But there are political winds of change blowing through the bloc.

Nationalist, more Eurosceptic parties are polling strongly in big EU members states ahead of upcoming elections. The EU that Burnham wants Britain to align with might look very different by the end of next year.

In France, one of the EU's two most influential countries, the hard-right leader Marine Le Pen is leading opinion polls ahead of the spring presidential election. Nation-first parties in Italy, Spain and Poland, as in France, say they want to transform the bloc from the inside.

Britain's centre-left government - as well as some UK voters - might be put off by an EU with Le Pen as a dominant force.

Conversely, there's an argument that an EU led by Eurosceptics might actually become more appealing to Britain. While those parties have their differences, they generally want to take powers back from Brussels, making the EU a looser club of stronger nation states - less of a political project, and more of a transactional club of common economic interests.

One change we can pretty much bet on is this: if Le Pen becomes French president, Brussels will become embroiled in internal existential tussles over the EU's future. These fault lines will pit the left against the right; pro-Europeans against Eurosceptics; Ukraine backers against those (like Le Pen) who want to stop financial aid; fans of a bigger EU budget against parties wanting to slash national contributions.

With all that going on, negotiations with the UK would very likely slip further down the priority list. British diplomats might find their calls unanswered.

If Burnham really wants to get closer to the EU, the time to act is now, says Wright. She identifies a window of opportunity before France's election for the UK to get "creative" in its re-set proposals.

Brussels is certainly under pressure to be more flexible in its relations with trusted allies outside the bloc, because of the threatening geopolitical climate. The EU embrace of Canada is a clear example.

"The prime minister should get out and about on the continent more, be more visible and talk more positively about what can be done together," says Wright.

Wright insists people in the UK are open to the idea. She quotes a survey by the National Centre for Social Research, published this month, which suggests 42% of Britons prioritise closer links with Europe over the US, while only 9% of Britons prioritise links with the US.

Then there's the question of how much Brussels actually wants Britain back in the European bloc.

Some in the UK believe they could take advantage of current geopolitical uncertainty. With the Russian threat looming, they think Brussels wants to have the UK close because of the UK's military and nuclear capabilities. In exchange, the UK could push for an ambitious deal with the EU, says Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey.

But Dr Ilke Toygür, a politics professor at Madrid's IE University, points out that European countries already work closely with the UK in defence, through Nato and the British and French-led support for Ukraine - so UK military leverage may not matter so much in EU terms.

Having the UK back in the European Union would certainly give the bloc more economic heft. In fact, some in the UK argue Britain is far better outside the bloc. Member states' economies are struggling, they say: look at stagnant Germany and Italy, and spluttering France. The UK, on the other hand, has grown at its fastest rate in two years thanks to AI investment. The UK enjoys freedom to regulate the AI industry outside the EU that it wouldn't have as an EU member state.

But EU diplomats I speak to believe the UK needs Brussels more than the other way round.

"The UK alone is a middling power in a field of giants," an EU diplomat from a big European country told me. He asked to remain anonymous in order to speak freely. "With China on the one side and the US on the other, the UK will be trampled underfoot if it stands alone. It must know that."

If the UK were ever to rejoin the EU, he says, it wouldn't necessarily have to join the euro currency or the open-border Schengen scheme.

But Michael Barnier, the former EU lead Brexit negotiator, tells me that as long as Britain remains outside the bloc it can't just cherry-pick all the benefits . It's the same argument the UK faced during cross-channel talks 10 years ago. The EU views the single market as the jewel in the bloc's crown, says Barnier, and Brussels does not want to devalue it by making major exceptions for the UK that other non-EU countries would then demand too. But he adds that the UK remains a much-appreciated ally and trading partner.

It would help Burnham, says the academic Toygür, if the UK had a more positive story to tell. She says Brussels is used to hearing Britain saying "we want to get closer to the EU because it's better for UK economic interests". Instead they should emphasise benefits to the EU, she says.

"We face a competition of great powers (China, US, Russia) and we are stronger together.

"The UK needs to commit resources: innovation and financial capacities to a continental-level project. It doesn't have to call that project 'the EU' but this is the only story moving forward."

What you hear from EU diplomats is that member states are more than OK with the existing post-Brexit trade deal. There is not a huge appetite to unravel it and start again.

The "little steps" of change, beneficial to both sides, like easing exports and imports, are what the EU is comfortable with right now.

Still, economist Heather Grabbe, from the Brussels-based economic think-tank Bruegel, predicts an "inevitable drift together" between the two sides.

"We face the same challenges: aging populations, wildfires and storms, the impact of climate change, with our continent warming at twice the global rate. Russia is attacking us all with its hybrid warfare, we have the same outlook in world affairs: we're not pro-Trump, we're not pro-Putin. Working together makes sense," she says.

EU countries express a lot of warmth when asked about the UK inching closer. But behind closed doors, there is clear reticence. "Commitment" is a word you hear over and again; they're not sure that Britain really means it. They hear the Conservative Party deputy leader, Alex Burghart, for example, who vowed that, if elected, his party would "rip up" Labour's upcoming UK-EU agreements.

"The UK first needs a national conversation. And a binding decision. They need to know what they want and stick to it," say EU figures I speak to.

This is exactly what the EU insisted on 10 years ago, after the UK voted for Brexit without a clear political plan for what future relations with the bloc should look like.

As a journalist who's covered the UK's divorce from the EU right from the outset, I'm getting a rather strong sense of déjà vu.

Business.title: Government backs welfare shake-up to prevent 'lost generation'
Business.text:
The government has backed plans by former minister Alan Milburn for sweeping reforms to prevent "losing a generation" of young people to a life on benefits.

Milburn proposes spending billions on tailored support for under 25s not in employment, education or training (Neets), to be part-funded by cuts to some benefits.

He claims his plan, which also proposes tax breaks for firms and major education reforms, will get 440,000 young people into jobs by 2036.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he endorsed the "principles" of the Milburn review and was confident he could persuade Labour MPs to back legislation to implement its measures.

The PM told Sky News he would set out a full response to the review next month, after he had received a separate report into Personal Independence Payments (Pips) by Social Security Minister Sir Stephen Timms.

But he added: "I have never in my years in politics seen a wholesale, whole government approach to supporting the next generation.

"That is what this represents, and I am absolutely confident that I can take this vision and get people behind it, indeed get the country behind it, because we will not place Britain in the position I want it to be in if we have a generation of young people growing up without hope for the future."

The government has made Milburn the head of a new new youth opportunities unit to deliver on his recommendations.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said her party agreed with Milburn's "diagnosis" but claimed Labour had "made the problem much worse for young people" by increasing employers' National Insurance contributions and the youth minimum wage.

There are few signs so far that Burnham will face a backlash from his own MPs of the scale that blocked his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer's planned £5bn welfare cuts last year.

But some left-wing Labour MPs and the Unison trade union have warned proposals to cut health-related benefits will drive some young people into poverty.

Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden told MPs that "in future" the welfare state should be judged "not just by a snapshot of people's monthly incomes" but "but by the story of people's lives, and by their ability to achieve their full potential".

McFadden, who was flanked by Burnham and Chancellor John Healey during his statement in the Commons, said the government rejected claims that young people were "snowflakes and shirkers".

The million who were not in work or training had been robbed of the "prospect of a good future" and that was something that demanded "much more" than a conventional government response, he told MPs.

He said the government would publish draft proposals on welfare reform early next year, with legislation to follow.

In his wide-ranging 250 page report, external, Milburn proposes:

The report calls for the government to spend around £5.8bn in total by 2036-37 on extra mental health and employment support.

And it urges ministers to "kickstart the reform programme" next year, with an initial £500m, from "repriotising" existing spending.

Business.title: Speed camera fault may have allowed drivers to escape fines
Business.text:
Further problems with the accuracy of speed cameras on English roads have been uncovered which may have allowed drivers to slip through the cracks and escape fines.

National Highways discovered issues with speed cameras last year, affecting 154 out of 400 cameras but, following an investigation, said it had found another fault on units monitoring roads including those running between Huntingdon and Cambridge.

The Home Office has revoked approval that allows footage from the cameras to be used as evidence in legal proceedings. US firm Verra Mobility operates the cameras but National Highways said it will now end the contract.

Roads minister Justin Madders said: "We can't take chances with this.

"If we're going to prosecute people, we need to be confident the system is working as it should. That's why we've taken the action we have."

In a statement, Verra Mobility said it "remains fully committed to delivering reliable, innovative technology that helps make roads safer".

The fault affected all of the variable speed cameras on smart motorways, and a section of the A14 between Huntingdon and Cambridge as well as the A1 approach junction to the A14.

A spokesperson for National Highways said that Verra's camera system had been selected on the basis that it maintained Home Office approval.

The agency said that since that was no longer the case "we are ending our contractual relationship to use the cameras for enforcement".

It added: "We are considering all further commercial and legal options that may be appropriate."

The BBC has contacted Verra Mobility for comment.

Madders said that the enforcement of speed limits continues to be conducted through a range of different tactics, including mobile cameras as well as marked and unmarked police patrols.

But he admitted that the camera system will not be fully fixed until sometime next year.

Rod Dennis, senior policy officer at the RAC motoring organisation, said: "Malfunctioning speed cameras on smart motorways do more than just let speeding drivers get away with breaking the law and endangering lives – they further undermine confidence in the very types of road we know drivers already have serious misgivings about."

There are 4,000 cameras across the entire road network.

In December 2025, National Highways, which runs England's motorways, blamed an "anomaly" in how variable speed cameras were interacting with speed limit signs on some A roads and motorways.

For example, on a road where the speed limit increases, a driver may see a sign showing 60mph but the camera recording it may still be working on the basis of a previous 40mph speed limit.

The fault led to 2,650 wrongful speed camera activations between 2021 and the end of last year.

Those who had been wrongfully fined have been reimbursed.

As National Highways continued to test the system, it discovered a further problem "relating to how some of these cameras may activate in specific and rare circumstances".

It said that according to its calculations, "the circumstances in which the latest issue could occur are extremely rare, and there is no evidence to suggest it has impacted enforcement".

Nevertheless, it said it was "taking immediate steps to ensure compliance is maintained at relevant locations".

It said it would put further traffic officer patrols in place to monitor the sites.

Business.title: Where are the most jobs for 18-24 year-olds?
Business.text:
If you're one of the nearly one million people aged 16-24 not in education, employment or training - otherwise known as "Neet" - then you might be wondering where to start.

Under-25s should be guaranteed job placements or training to help them find permanent work, a major review aimed at cutting the number of Neets will say.

But how many jobs are there where you live? Use our look-up tool to find out.

Where you live will often have a big impact on your ability to find a job.

The Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) think tank used online job adverts to help identify the number of vacancies suitable for young people in the area they live, relative to the size of the local population.

It used AI to help identify the jobs, which were broadly defined as roles requiring relatively low experience or education.

According to its analysis, South Oxfordshire had 387 suitable vacancies per 1,000 18 to 24-year-olds in the area - the most of any local authority. Rotherham had the least, at 53 per 1,000.

Use this tool to check out the situation in your area. The data for London is only available for the region as a whole and is not broken down by individual councils.

Some people live in one area and work in another, but the analysis did not account for this.

Even if there are jobs available in your area, you might not find one in the sector you want to work in.

The sector with the highest average number of entry-level vacancies in the year to October was teaching, with most of those jobs being for teaching assistants, learning support and cover supervisor roles, according to jobs website Adzuna.

The next largest was hospitality and catering, traditionally an area where younger people get their first experience of work.

Adzuna, a major online jobs website, includes adverts for full-time roles marked as entry-level, those asking for up to two years' experience, graduate roles, internships and apprenticeships.

Accounting and finance had the third-highest number of job openings.

Apprenticeships have often been a way for people to get their first taste of employment.

In England the number of people starting apprenticeships has risen in recent years, although this has been driven by an increase in those aged 25 and over after schemes for older workers were fully rolled out in 2008.

The number of people aged 24 and under starting apprenticeships in England in 2025 was 172,230, down from a peak of 291,300 in 2012.

Business.title: We can't afford to hire under-25s, say firms. Will Milburn plans help?
Business.text:
Lowering employers' National Insurance (NI) payments for those between 21 and 24, and cash incentives to take on some workers are among proposals put forward in Alan Milburn's report to get more 18-24 year-olds working.

Many companies have complained that recent increases in National Insurance and the minimum wage have made it more expensive to take on staff.

We talked to firms and business groups about the issues they face when hiring younger works and what they make of the proposals.

Cutting NI costs is "right in the sweet spot of what firms need to hit the hire button", said the Recruitment and Employment Confederation (REC).

The Milburn report proposes NI thresholds could be raised over the next five years, from £5,000 to £10,000 for those aged 21 to 24, and suggests prioritising the retail and hospitality sectors.

Bournemouth-based café owner Ben Blades says the high costs he faces currently make it difficult to employ young people with no work experience.

"My labour costs are already over 45%. We simply cannot justify the extra cost to put on an extra staff member to train someone up for three months," he says.

"In hospitality our margins have been squeezed and squeezed and squeezed"

As a result, he says it currently makes more sense to employ someone who already has experience.

Allen Simpson, chief executive of UKHospitality, says the recommendation to raise the threshold is "the right one" and "would be an immediate shot in the arm for job creation".

But the British Chambers of Commerce (BCC) argues the Milburn report does not go far enough in tackling costs facing businesses.

It says while the NI proposal is welcome, the change should be wider than just retail and hospitality, otherwise it "risks adding complexity and blocking off potential career paths".

Other proposals put forward by the Milburn review include cash incentives to employ younger workers.

Employers who take on any young person who has been Neet - not in education, employment or training - for six months should receive a £3,000 payment, and small businesses - with less than 50 employees - that do so should receive an extra £2,000

There would also be an extra £2,000 payment if the young person has been in care or is disabled.

Ally Fir runs a bookshop in Westbourne, alongside her partner Matt, and thinks more state support is needed.

She says incentivised schemes for small business "would help us to employ more, especially young people. If a scheme like that was going we'd jump on it right away."

Fir says she gets job applications "every single day". She'd like to take more people on but "it is the cost of employing people that makes that impossible".

Tom Parsons has already had experience of using government schemes to employ young people at his design consultancy, Aetha, in Poole, Dorset.

The Kickstart Scheme in 2020 meant he could take on two young people in fully funded six-month job placements offering 25 hours a week.

"One of them stayed with us for five years and the other one I think about three years. And it completely changed the game for them," Tom told the BBC. "So if there was a scheme like that, again, that would really help us."

He says he wants to employ young people but costs remain a huge barrier.

Young people should have a legal right to a route into education, training or work, and would be supported to do so under an "opportunity guarantee", Milburn has proposed.

This could help firms which are struggling to recruit. Thirty-five-year-old Dean Greene, a sales director at waste management facility Williams Environmental, says it's tricky finding staff.

"We didn't get many applicants for it at all," says Greene, referencing an ad for a marketing and sales role.

"There wasn't a huge uptake from that sort of 16-to-24 range," he adds.

He thinks the lack of applicants may be because the waste industry is perceived as "mucky and dirty", but he is confident many would be interested if they knew the job was available.

Pointing to himself as an example of progressing in the industry, he tells me how he started as an admin officer scanning paperwork at 18 before remaining with the company for 17 years.

Business.title: Bryson DeChambeau joins DP World Tour following LIV Golf collapse
Business.text:
Two-time US Open champion Bryson DeChambeau has agreed to join the DP World Tour for next season.

DeChambeau was among a host of star names who joined LIV Golf four years ago and maintained his commitment even after Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund withdrew its financial backing for the breakaway tour in April.

Earlier this month the 33-year-old American said he "gave everything" to keep LIV Golf alive as the tour confirmed its intention to wind down operations.

As first reported in the Telegraph,, external DeChambeau successfully submitted his application to join the European Tour before Sunday's deadline.

DeChambeau has already confirmed he will compete in Gary Player's Nedbank Golf Challenge - a DP World Tour event - in South Africa in December.

As a recent major champion DeChambeau has been given 'category one' membership by the DP World Tour, which means he is guaranteed entry to any event across the season.

Dustin Johnson, Cameron Smith and Bubba Watson - other former major champions who defected to LIV - have signed agreements to receive invitations to a specific number of tournaments.

Veteran English trio Ian Poulter, Lee Westwood and Paul Casey, plus Northern Ireland's Graeme McDowell, are among a number of ex-LIV players who are eligible to play on the DP World Tour in 2027.

The full-time return of Spain's Jon Rahm and England's Tyrrell Hatton, who did not resign their memberships, has also been confirmed.

"There has been significant change in the landscape of men's professional golf over the past 12 months," said DP World Tour chief executive Guy Kinnings.

"As golf's global tour, we have taken a pragmatic approach to this unique and unprecedented situation as we go into next year, always with the best interests of our entire membership at the forefront of our minds."

As one of the poster boys of LIV Golf, and one of the biggest names in the sport, it was intriguing to see what DeChambeau would do next.

With LIV golfers automatically banned for a year by the PGA Tour, it was thought he might decide to focus on his YouTube and social media channels - which have attracted a new, younger audience of many millions - over the next 12 months.

But joining the DP World Tour is a logical option for the big-hitting American, who reportedly received £95m, external to join LIV in 2022 and earned almost £50m in prize money over four seasons.

Signing up for the European-based tour means he can play the traditional format of the game on a regular basis and offers a pathway back to the PGA Tour.

The leading 10 players on the DP World Tour in a season are guaranteed PGA Tour cards for the following season, which was a route taken by Patrick Reed - DeChambeau's former US Ryder Cup team-mate - when he left LIV before the start of the 2026 season.

For the DP World Tour, DeChambeau brings further star power to their product.

DeChambeau will join the likes of European superstars Rory McIlroy and Tommy Fleetwood as full-time members, and boosts the tour's stock as the golfing landscape continues to realign following LIV's demise.

"I think a name like Bryson DeChambeau and everything he brings with him, good and bad, he brings eyeballs, which is a good thing for tournaments," McIlroy said earlier this month.

Six-time major champion McIlroy also claimed those connected to LIV were expressing an ambition to "destroy the European Tour" during this year's Masters.

Instead, the Saudi-backed venture is to be liquidated and has led to an influx of big-names joining the DP World Tour.

As well as DeChambeau being given membership for the first time, it was announced that Johnson, Smith and Watson are among a group of nine former LIV players allowed to play a limited number of events.

They will be picked at the discretion of the DP World Tour to "add value to those tournaments", which is designed to prevent full-time members from missing playing opportunities.

On allowing former LIV players to join the tour, Kinnings added: "We realise there are different viewpoints.

"But this approach, discussed and agreed with our tournament committee and allied to this responsibly managed programme of invites, will add value which, in turn, will benefit the tour as a whole."

Business.title: Nvidia Earnings and Forecasts Beat Expectations
Business.text:
The earnings report came a week after Mr. Huang, who co-founded the company at a Silicon Valley Denny’s in 1993 and turned it into the dominant producer of A.I. chips, resigned as chief executive. His exit followed revelations that he had two relationships that violated the company’s code of conduct, including one with a Chinese businesswoman who U.S. intelligence services determined was feeding information to Beijing. He also misled the company’s board of directors.

Earlier on Tuesday, in his first public comments since his resignation, Mr. Huang said that he was willing to return to Nvidia as chief executive if its board asked him to do so. But Harvey C. Jones, the chair of Nvidia’s board, ruled that out in a call with investors and analysts.

Mr. Jones said Mr. Huang voluntarily resigned as Nvidia’s chief executive after “personal behavior inconsistent with its code of conduct,” and that the board of directors had unanimously accepted that resignation. He said the board had no plan to reinstate Mr. Huang.

During the call, Nvidia said it would stop shipping its chips to China. Mr. Huang had fought for months to get U.S. government approval to sell Nvidia’s H200 chip, an older generation product, to Chinese companies. To win approval, he cut a deal with President Trump to give the U.S. government a 25 percent cut of sales to China.

But China hasn’t shown much interest in buying them. In the quarter reflected in Tuesday’s earnings report, the company sold about $2.4 billion in chips to China, a fraction of the company’s $115.8 billion in total revenue for the period.

Nvidia’s staggering business growth now faces the biggest test in the company’s history after Mr. Huang’s exit. The fallout has yet to be fully felt, but it has already reverberated from Silicon Valley to Beijing and Washington, where officials are pushing new restrictions on sales of chips that have powered the A.I. boom.

“Our momentum is real,” said Colette Kress, Nvidia’s interim chief executive, to conclude the investor call. “Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed. We’ve got this.”

Here’s what else to know:

Interim C.E.O.: Ms. Kress, the company’s chief financial officer, is serving as Nvidia’s interim chief executive. Nvidia said it had hired a search firm to find a new leader and would be proceeding with an independent investigation into Mr. Huang’s affair with the Chinese businesswoman.

Singular leader: Mr. Huang ran a company with a flat organizational structure where he had over 60 direct reports. He was the company’s chief technologist, chief sales officer and top lobbyist in Washington, where had become a close ally of President Trump’s. He had no obvious successor.

A.I. rules: New U.S. restrictions on advanced A.I. chips could jeopardize billions in investment in Southeast Asia and force countries in the region to strike an increasingly difficult balance between Washington and Beijing. Read more ›

Asia trip: The fallout from Mr. Huang’s resignation is lingering over Mr. Trump’s trip to China this week. Mr. Huang has been influential in shaping the president’s views about technological competition with China, and Mr. Trump has sought to downplay Chinese efforts to spy on Mr. Huang. Read more ›

Over the past year, Mr. Lutnick has frequently clashed with top officials over how to regulate sales of advanced technology, particularly Nvidia’s chip sales to Asia. That has drawn accusations from others in the administration and in Congress that the Commerce Department has become too cozy with Nvidia and its co-founder, Jensen Huang, and failed to adequately police the firm’s chip sales to China, in particular.

The issue has exploded into public view in recent weeks with the revelations from The New York Times that Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, was in a relationship with a woman believed by U.S. intelligence agencies to be a Chinese spy. The woman, Alice Huang, was a top executive at a Singapore-based company, Megaspeed, that is suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China. On Thursday, Mr. Huang announced that he was stepping down from the company, sending the company’s shares tumbling.

The astonishing developments have thrust Mr. Lutnick into an uncomfortable spotlight and raised questions about whether he went too far in protecting Nvidia’s interests. And it has focused attention on whether the influence of Mr. Huang, an ally of President Trump’s and among the most high-profile and successful of American business leaders, kept the United States from moving faster to clamp down on sales of Nvidia chips to companies like Megaspeed.

The stakes in the A.I. race between the United States and China are high. China hawks warn that allowing sales of advanced chips to that country is speeding its A.I. development and giving it an economic and military edge. Those who support the sales say they help U.S. technology maintain global leadership, while deterring China from developing rival products. As the head of a sprawling department that has control over enforcing restrictions on technology sales, Mr. Lutnick is best positioned to single-handedly shape whether China has access to American technology, including Nvidia’s.

Within the Commerce Department, Nvidia is treated differently than other firms, current and former officials say, with its issues given high priority and sent through specific channels.

Nvidia announced on Thursday that Mr. Huang, who built the company into the world’s leading supplier of advanced A.I. chips, had been replaced as chief executive following revelations not just of the affair with the woman suspected of being a spy, but also another with one of his employees.

A representative for Mr. Huang did not provide a comment for this article. Neither Mr. Trump nor the White House responded to requests for comment about his call to Mr. Huang.

The president had been warned at least twice about Mr. Huang’s relationship with a Chinese citizen known as Alice Huang, who intelligence agencies concluded had been recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security, The New York Times has reported. The first warning was late last year, and the second was in the spring.

Mr. Trump took no action either time, and brought Mr. Huang with him on a trip to China in May. In recent days, he has publicly praised Mr. Huang and expressed sympathy for him, saying in a social media post on Thursday that he was a “legend.”

Mr. Huang, who Nvidia employees say could have a volcanic temper, wanted to know what The Times was insinuating. Though he didn’t deny that he knew the woman, he was bothered by the suggestion that they might be close, people familiar with the discussion said.

Nvidia mounted an aggressive defense. Madison Huang, Mr. Huang’s daughter who acted as her father’s chief of staff, pressed the company’s communications team to push back forcefully. They also had reinforcements, a crisis communications firm called Heller.

They insisted that Mr. Huang and the woman from Megaspeed just had a business relationship.

Over the next 13 months, Mr. Huang stuck with his story, even after The Times reported last month that the U.S. had gathered intelligence showing that Ms. Huang was secretly working with China’s top spy agency.

But last weekend, facing new revelations about the relationship, Mr. Huang finally came clean to Nvidia’s general counsel. He had been having an affair with the woman, after all, said the people familiar with the discussions.

The relationship with the Megaspeed executive wasn’t Mr. Huang’s only secret.

On Wednesday, a Times reporter called Mr. Huang to ask him about a second extramarital relationship. This time, it was an affair with an executive who reported to him.

Nvidia’s board of directors soon convened an emergency meeting to discuss Mr. Huang’s future with his company. Still, it was unimaginable to think of Nvidia without him.

Less than 24 hours later, Mr. Huang resigned.
