Mr. Trump took no action either time, and brought Mr. Huang with him on a trip to China in May. In recent days, he has publicly praised Mr. Huang and expressed sympathy for him, saying in a social media post on Thursday that he was a “legend.”

Mr. Huang, who Nvidia employees say could have a volcanic temper, wanted to know what The Times was insinuating. Though he didn’t deny that he knew the woman, he was bothered by the suggestion that they might be close, people familiar with the discussion said.

Nvidia mounted an aggressive defense. Madison Huang, Mr. Huang’s daughter who acted as her father’s chief of staff, pressed the company’s communications team to push back forcefully. They also had reinforcements, a crisis communications firm called Heller.

They insisted that Mr. Huang and the woman from Megaspeed just had a business relationship.

Over the next 13 months, Mr. Huang stuck with his story, even after The Times reported last month that the U.S. had gathered intelligence showing that Ms. Huang was secretly working with China’s top spy agency.

But last weekend, facing new revelations about the relationship, Mr. Huang finally came clean to Nvidia’s general counsel. He had been having an affair with the woman, after all, said the people familiar with the discussions.

The relationship with the Megaspeed executive wasn’t Mr. Huang’s only secret.

On Wednesday, a Times reporter called Mr. Huang to ask him about a second extramarital relationship. This time, it was an affair with an executive who reported to him.

Nvidia’s board of directors soon convened an emergency meeting to discuss Mr. Huang’s future with his company. Still, it was unimaginable to think of Nvidia without him.

Less than 24 hours later, Mr. Huang resigned.

The earnings report came a week after Mr. Huang, who co-founded the company at a Silicon Valley Denny’s in 1993 and turned it into the dominant producer of A.I. chips, resigned as chief executive. His exit followed revelations that he had two relationships that violated the company’s code of conduct, including one with a Chinese businesswoman who U.S. intelligence services determined was feeding information to Beijing. He also misled the company’s board of directors.

Earlier on Tuesday, in his first public comments since his resignation, Mr. Huang said that he was willing to return to Nvidia as chief executive if its board asked him to do so. But Harvey C. Jones, the chair of Nvidia’s board, ruled that out in a call with investors and analysts.

Mr. Jones said Mr. Huang voluntarily resigned as Nvidia’s chief executive after “personal behavior inconsistent with its code of conduct,” and that the board of directors had unanimously accepted that resignation. He said the board had no plan to reinstate Mr. Huang.

During the call, Nvidia said it would stop shipping its chips to China. Mr. Huang had fought for months to get U.S. government approval to sell Nvidia’s H200 chip, an older generation product, to Chinese companies. To win approval, he cut a deal with President Trump to give the U.S. government a 25 percent cut of sales to China.

But China hasn’t shown much interest in buying them. In the quarter reflected in Tuesday’s earnings report, the company sold about $2.4 billion in chips to China, a fraction of the company’s $115.8 billion in total revenue for the period.

Nvidia’s staggering business growth now faces the biggest test in the company’s history after Mr. Huang’s exit. The fallout has yet to be fully felt, but it has already reverberated from Silicon Valley to Beijing and Washington, where officials are pushing new restrictions on sales of chips that have powered the A.I. boom.

“Our momentum is real,” said Colette Kress, Nvidia’s interim chief executive, to conclude the investor call. “Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed. We’ve got this.”

Sports.title: Cricket Australia sets up 'safe space' for players to share sandpapergate experiences
Sports.text:
Cricket Australia has launched an independent "forum" for players and staff involved in the sandpapergate scandal to share their version of events.

In a memoir released earlier this month, former player Usman Khawaja claimed the entire Australia team knew of the plot to tamper with the ball during a 2018 Test in South Africa, contradicting the investigation at the time.

His comments have led to a bitter split among former and current players and have overshadowed the beginning of Australia's international cricket season.

The forum was not a new investigation and there will be no new penalties, Cricket Australia said, adding that nobody would be forced to take part.

However, chief executive Todd Greenberg said he hoped the discussions would allow the sport to "move on".

"The game is genuinely hurting at the moment. It's not good for anyone," he said.

"We need to find a path through and we need some time to heal."

The sandpapergate scandal is often described as one of Australian cricket's darkest days and was a source of national shame.

An expedited investigation at the time found three players knew about the plan: captain Steve Smith, vice-captain David Warner and fellow batter Cameron Bancroft. They all faced lengthy bans.

However Khawaja, Warner and another player on the tour, Chadd Sayers, have all now said they believe everyone knew.

Current Australia captain Pat Cummins has rejected claims he knew sandpaper was being taken onto the field as "nonsense", and expressed hurt that Khawaja - his friend - had called his reputation into question.

The release of Khawaja's book has also renewed scrutiny of Cricket Australia's initial investigation. A handful of players - including the batter - have said they were not interviewed for it, and Warner has accused the governing body of a "cover-up".

"Over the past week we've had several different and conflicting accounts of what transpired in Cape Town in 2018 and it's been an incredibly difficult and uncomfortable time for the game and for everyone who was involved," Greenberg said on Wednesday.

"What's become clear is that some players were not heard at that time. That opportunity now exists in a place without judgement, without sanction."

Terms of reference for the forum are being drafted, he said, and a former judge or "someone of that ilk" will be recruited to run it, confidentially and independently.

No deadline has been set, but Greenberg said he hoped the discussions could be completed "quickly", at which time the Cricket Australia board would decide what information to make public.

"We will look to be as transparent as we possibly can, whilst at the same time protecting the confidentiality of the people who come forward."

The incident had "a lot to do with the culture that existed back at the time", Greenberg said: a win-at-all-costs mentality which he admitted the governing body played a role in creating.

He added that it is important the current Australian team be "afforded the space to perform at their best at what is a very important time and period for the game".

Though players like Khawaja and Warner have retired from international cricket, Australia's bowling attack in the contentious third Test - Pat Cummins, Josh Hazlewood, Nathan Lyon and Mitchell Starc - remain fixtures in the national side. So too does Steve Smith, who returned to the team in 2019.

Khawaja, who is commentating Australia's one-day international against England in Hobart on Wednesday alongside Warner, welcomed the announcement.

"I wish Cricket Australia would have done this a week-and-a-half ago, probably longer ago," Khawaja said on streamer Kayo Sports.

"My questions will always be 'what is the outcome from this?'"

Warner said Australians deserved an "open public inquiry" instead.

"Because we have no idea about what's happened behind closed doors with CA [Cricket Australia]."

Former player turned coach Jason Gillespie and Darren Lehmann - who coached Australia at the time of the scandal - both said the forum was a good idea.

"Let's not beat around the bush - they didn't have a choice. Cricket Australia had to do something, the drums were beating louder and louder," Gillespie told the broadcaster ABC.

"I haven't been great and the people close to me know that... The last couple of weeks have been tough, but they have been for everyone," Lehmann added.

Sports.title: Nations League: Belief and bench help Northern Ireland to League A promotion
Sports.text:
After going 500 minutes without conceding a goal, Northern Ireland could be forgiven for having to make adjustments to play from behind.

Having travelled to Budapest knowing a point against Hungary would be enough to top Nations League B2, Barnabas Varga's strike after 35 minutes for the hosts at the Puskas Arena altered the picture and, for the first time in the campaign, left Michael O'Neill's side having to chase a game.

Their response to the deficit - on the pitch, from the bench and high in the stands where their suspended manager was watching the game - displayed the best characteristics of a side who had not won at this level before this unbeaten campaign.

While the point from a 1-1 draw in Budapest will be long remembered for Justin Devenny's brilliant equaliser and the scenes of celebration that greeted promotion to the competition's top tier for the first time, it was beyond the highlights and headlines that O'Neill saw the emerging qualities of his side.

"We went behind tonight and it was difficult, you know? Big stadium, big atmosphere, but we came out and played well in the second half and got what we needed from the game," said the manager.

"Those are things that I'm very pleased that are in this squad at such a young age. The technical side of the game we'll always look to improve on, but in terms of the physical, the tactical and the mental side of a game, we're very far ahead of where I thought we would be at this time."

Hungary enjoyed more than 70% possession in the first half, and they could have been further than a goal ahead with Liverpool star Dominik Szoboszlai striking the base of the post after only five minutes.

O'Neill made his first change at half-time, bringing on veteran striker Josh Magennis, while Kieran Morrison, Brodie Spencer and Paul Smyth all followed in the second half.

Magennis and Morrison made a real impact before the equaliser, but it was the belief shown by all involved that O'Neill felt was key to the turnaround.

"I felt in the first half from where I was seeing the game, we just looked a little bit leggy which is natural," added O'Neill.

"I just felt we needed that freshness at the right points in the game that helped us, but it was the belief that we could get back into the game, and the belief that we could see the game out.

"I think we showed a lot of attributes that are in this squad at this moment in time and certainly in the second half that was that was the case."

For all the plaudits earned by this team who conceded just one goal in six games while picking up 12 points, among the most impressive aspects of the campaign has been who they have had to do without.

Talismanic Liverpool defender Conor Bradley has not played for this side in over 12 months through injury.

Ali McCann is another who missed both 2026 Nations League windows, while influential defender Daniel Ballard featured only in the first game in Georgia before a hamstring injury.

Arsenal's Ceadach O'Neill was forced to pull out of the November squad through injury at a time when he would perhaps have been the most natural replacement for Jamie Donley after the striker picked up a second booking against Ukraine last week and had to miss the finale through suspension.

Having taken over an ageing squad four years ago, O'Neill has rebuilt his playing panel with a group that feels as if it is getting deeper with each international window.

"The encouraging thing is we have players on the outside - we've Bradley to come back in, Ballard to come back in, Ali McCann, young Ceadach, Eoin Toal," added the former Stoke City and Blackburn Rovers boss.

"We have good competition for places now. We're going to need that competition, and some players are going to miss out, but we are building depth to the squad that will help us going forward."

Come the next Nations League, that will be all the way into the uncharted territory of the top tier.

Sports.title: Craig Bellamy: Wales boss takes belief from Nations League campaign
Sports.text:
Craig Bellamy kept coming back to one word. Belief.

His Wales side had just lost a fifth game out of six to finish bottom of their Nations League group. Bellamy would have been forgiven for feeling a little bruised.

But there are ways of losing and ways of finishing bottom.

Wales were fearless against Portugal, exhilarating in attack and proving they can compete at the highest level of this competition, even as they were beaten 3-2 in Cardiff.

And while they were already consigned to the foot of the Group A4 table, Wales' previous performances mean they at least have the back-up of a relegation play-off in March to preserve their top-flight status.

"Belief's the biggest one," Bellamy said when he was asked what he and his team had taken from this campaign.

"Not just this game, but in general. We are beyond close to this level. We can more than compete at this level.

"We demand and want to expect to be. Getting into League A is big for us, but also staying in A is going to allow us to develop.

"You can only develop and improve by playing the best teams, and I felt we've taken another shift."

Wales have certainly fared better than they did when they were last in the top tier of the Nations League, when they finished with one point from six games and were relegated.

Victory against World Cup quarter-finalists Norway last month was their first at this level and, had they been more clinical in Oslo on Saturday, they might have got a second win of the campaign.

Ultimately, Wales' inability to take their chances – combined with sloppy defensive mistakes – meant their results did not match their performances.

And the reality is that they were up against stellar opposition, whose vastly superior resources showed with their greater ruthlessness at both ends of the pitch.

"If there's anything you would have learned from these games, then you see killers. That's why they're at the top," Bellamy added.

"I know people look at results. I'm fully aware of the business. This is all I know. But I think when you look at reality as well, and you look at our performances during this group, I couldn't ask for more.

"I feel we're closer than probably maybe the players thought they were. It's fine margins.

"But I feel the biggest word out of this now has been belief, really, for me."

Wales had the best record of the four teams who finished bottom of their top-flight groups, meaning they have a second chance to avoid relegation in the form of a two-leg play-off in March.

At Friday's draw in Switzerland, Bellamy's side will discover whether they will face Slovenia, Hungary, Republic of Ireland or Bosnia-Herzegovina, who beat them in a World Cup play-off earlier this year.

Those teams all finished second in their League B groups and, as the League A team, Wales will have home advantage in the second leg.

"Going into the next one, we have to be in this group," said Bellamy. "If we want to develop as a football nation and keep going forward, we have to be playing against the best teams. It's only going to improve you.

"I know we can go back to League B... It's about playing the best teams. That's how we're going to get better. I honestly believe it."

Bellamy, who has a contract running to 2028, said: "I won't be here for the next Nations League. I won't be the manager then. So I'm doing it for the next one, but I'm also doing it for the players.

"We've got to. That's how we're going to be the best version of us and keep improving."

Sports.title: Wayne Rooney: Ex-Manchester United captain considered taking own life during playing career
Sports.text:
Warning: This article contains references to suicide

Wayne Rooney says he was "contemplating suicide" during his playing days at Manchester United and was "speaking to a therapist to try and figure out what was up".

The former England captain joined United from Everton in 2004 and went on to become the club's record goalscorer, with 253 goals in 559 appearances.

But Rooney, speaking with Gabby Logan on the Life at the Midpoint podcast, external, detailed his struggles off the pitch when eldest son Kai, who is now 17, was a baby.

"When I was drinking, I would lock myself in my house for two days and just drink," said Rooney, when asked about the lowest point in his life.

"This is probably in my best part of my career playing wise."

The 41-year-old went on to explain how he "struggled to deal with it all" and, after opening up to his wife Coleen and his mother, knew he "needed help to get through it".

"I can look back and say I was selfish, but I knew I was going through something which I was really struggling to deal with," he added.

"I didn't want Kai seeing me like that, so that's why I'd hide away as well.

"I got to a place where you're contemplating suicide. I just didn't want to be around anyone. I didn't want to see people in the streets. I didn't want to go into shops.

"I was always comfortable on a football pitch, but everything else, [I] really struggled with it."

Rooney, who scored 53 goals in 120 England appearances, was recently named pundit of the year at the Broadcast Sport Awards and is currently appearing on reality TV show I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here.

He helped United win five Premier League titles, the Champions League, Europa League, FA Cup and three EFL Cups before leaving them to return to the Toffees in 2017.

But the former forward said he learned to mask his feelings during his lowest moments.

"You don't want to show any weakness, so you try to mask it," Rooney added.

"Even though I knew the position I was in, it was difficult to actually admit that I was in that position because I felt like you feel less of a man, if you like, for doing that.

"I was speaking to a therapist to try and figure out what was up with me because when I look back I was probably at the height of my career, I've just had a young son, I've just been married.

"It should be the happiest point in my life and it wasn't.

"It was probably the lowest point because of the selfish acts I was taking.

"Coleen helped me massively. She could have walked away, it was that bad, but she stuck by me and helped me get through it."

Sports.title: Rassie Erasmus: South Africa head coach banned for six matches following match official comments
Sports.text:
South Africa head coach Rassie Erasmus has been banned for six matches by World Rugby over comments he made about match officials in his side's Nations Championship defeat by France last week.

Speaking at a news conference conference in Dublin on Monday before the Springboks' match with Ireland, Erasmus questioned what he perceived as double standards in officiating to the point where he asked: "is that not match-fixing?".

The two-time Rugby World Cup-winning coach was referencing the implementation of new rules surrounding hip-drop and knee-drop tackles, and felt the laws were not being applied correctly.

It comes after Ireland fly-half Sam Prendergast became the first player to be cited for a hip-drop tackle in Ireland's win over Fiji on Saturday, which was not penalised in-play by referee Angus Gardner and television match official [TMO] Mike Adamson.

World Rugby said an independent panel determined that Erasmus' comments "suggest that match officials acted with bias/prejudice or deliberately influenced the outcome of a match".

In response, South Africa Rugby said it has requested a full misconduct hearing and an opportunity for Erasmus to "contextualise his comments and assure the panel that it was not his intention to allege that any match official had acted with ulterior motives".

It is the third time Erasmus has been sanctioned by World Rugby over his comments about match officials.

When he was South Africa's director of rugby, he was suspended for two months by World Rugby after he posted an hour-long video criticising the refereeing in the Springboks' opening Test defeat by the British and Irish Lions in 2021.

World Rugby found the video contained "multiple abusive and insulting comments and attacks on the officials".

In 2022, he received a two-match ban for a series of tweets criticising officials in a defeat by France.

Erasmus' latest ban has been imposed under World Rugby's match official abuse sanction process, which was introduced by the governing body in July.

If the suspension is upheld, Erasmus will miss Saturday's game with Ireland in Dublin (16:40 GMT), next week's finals weekend fixture at Twickenham's Allianz Stadium and the start of his side's Rugby Championship campaign next summer.

Erasmus said that 17 hip-drop or knee-drop tackles had been missed in South Africa's 21-19 defeat in France by match officials. Andrea Piardi was the referee for the Stade de France fixture, while Matteo Liperini was the TMO.

Erasmus added that if TMOs were not intervening for reviews to limit the number of interruptions during a match then it was "manipulation", before he added that his comments were "not an accusation".

"I'm saying if he didn't see it, it must be a technology problem. If he saw it and decided not to act on it, is that not match-fixing?" Erasmus added.

"If the TMO didn't see it, maybe then technology must be better. If he saw it and he ignored it, what does that boil down to? Manipulation of the game or the result or injured players getting injured.

"So all I'm asking, don't take TMOs out and discourage them to get involved. Then the wrong team will win and players will get injured. That's all I'm saying."

In a statement on Tuesday, World Rugby said an independent panel determined that Erasmus' comments had met "the threshold for serious misconduct".

World Rugby confirmed the ban will stop Erasmus having any match day involvement for six matches, which includes coaching, direct or indirect contact with the team management or players on match days, entering the stadium, coaches' box, playing enclosure or technical area.

"The panel determined that the comments suggest that match officials acted with bias/prejudice or deliberately influenced the outcome of a match, and when the conduct is considered as a whole a reasonable person would conclude that the conduct constituted an unacceptable attack on the credibility and competence of the match officials," its statement said.

"In respect to the sanction, the panel determined that the conduct clearly amounts to disrespecting the authority of the match officials by impugning their integrity.

"Therefore, the panel reviewed a number of elements of the commentary including the timing and reach of the statements, combined with the allegations of bias or bad faith, and found that the comments attracted a six-match automatic suspension."

This is the third time in five years Erasmus has been banned for comments about referees, all of them coming after a Springboks loss.

In 2018, he picked South African rugby up off the floor and has won two World Cups to establish himself as one of the greatest coaches of all time.

To his rugby public - the people who really matter in Erasmus' eyes - he will forever be a hero in his homeland.

But outside South Africa his propensity to harangue officials after a rare defeat will tarnish his reputation in the eyes of many.

Sports.title: Grand Slam of Darts results: Luke Humphries and Michael van Gerwen reach last 16
Sports.text:
Luke Humphries and Michael van Gerwen booked their places in the last 16 of the Grand Slam of Darts with victories in their final group matches.

Humphries beat fellow Englishman Joe Cullen 5-2 despite averaging 98.67 to his opponent's 103.22.

The former world champion will now face compatriot Tom Sykes, the lowest-ranked player remaining in the tournament, after he defeated Krzysztof Ratajski 5-1 to top Group J.

Van Gerwen was well below his best as he scraped past Sweden's Jeffrey de Graaf 5-4.

The Dutchman missed several match darts at 4-3 up, allowing De Graaf to force a deciding leg.

However, Van Gerwen regrouped to seal victory and set up a last-16 meeting with James Wade.

"It wasn't a good game at all. We were both under pressure and that didn't do us any favours," Van Gerwen said.

"Sometimes you don't do what you want to do. That's frustrating because I know I am capable of a lot more."

Elsewhere, Wade, Gian van Veen and Nathan Aspinall all made light work of their opponents to secure their places in the knockout stage.

Sports.title: BBC Women's Footballer of the Year 2026: Cast your vote now
Sports.text:
Voting for the BBC World Service Women's Footballer of the Year 2026 will close at 09:00 GMT on Wednesday, 18 November.

Fans worldwide can vote from the five-player shortlist of Temwa Chawinga, Ewa Pajor, Alexia Putellas, Alessia Russo and Khadija 'Bunny' Shaw.

For the first time in the award's history, the winner will be announced as part of the BBC's Sports Personality of the Year on Sunday, 13 December as well as on the BBC World Service and the BBC Sport website and app.

Contenders for the award - now in its 12th year - are nominated by coaches, journalists and former professionals. It covers the period September 2025-August 2026.

Cast your vote, and read more on the five contenders.

Age: 28 Country: Malawi

Club: Kansas City Position: Forward

Chawinga has established herself as one of the world's most prolific forwards.

Her impact on the National Women's Soccer League is clear. Her extraordinary form helped Kansas City Current clinch the NWSL Shield as the league's top team in the regular season.

Chawinga scored 15 goals in the 2025 season as she became the first player to be named NWSL MVP in back-to-back campaigns. She also won the Golden Boot for the second year in a row.

Those performances earned her a contract extension through until 2029.

Chawinga returned to international football with Malawi for the 2026 Women's Africa Cup of Nations.

Alongside her sister Tabitha, she helped Malawi reach the country's first Wafcon final and - in doing so - qualify for the Women's World Cup for the first time.

Chawinga scored against Nigeria, Egypt, Ghana and Algeria at Wafcon, winning the tournament's Golden Boot with five goals.

Age: 29 Country: Poland

Club: Barcelona Position: Forward

Pajor is widely regarded as a world-class number nine - and it's clear why.

Instrumental as Barcelona won four trophies last season, Pajor scored their first two goals in a 4-0 Champions League final victory over Lyon.

The goals meant she finished as the competition's top scorer, while the result meant she won the Champions League for the first time after losing in five finals - four with Wolfsburg and one with Barcelona.

Pajor also enjoyed an outstanding second season with Barcelona in Liga F, scoring 16 league goals in her 23 appearances and providing five assists. She was a key player as Barca won the domestic treble.

On the international stage, Pajor captains Poland and is the team's leading goalscorer.

Age: 32 Country: Spain

Club: London City Lionesses Position: Midfielder

Putellas showed again this year why she is one of the most influential footballers in the world.

After 14 years with Barcelona, she delivered a spectacular final season with the club - helping them win four major trophies.

Her 14 goal contributions in 11 Champions League appearances helped her childhood club win the competition for the fourth time, and she remained a decisive figure bringing experience and leadership when it mattered most.

Putellas delayed announcing her move to London City Lionesses to avoid creating a distraction, but in July 2026 she completed that transfer, saying the club's "women-only identity and ambition" were important factors.

Internationally, Putellas was instrumental in Spain retaining the Women's Nations League in late 2025, scoring three goals against Sweden in the semi-finals before being named player of the finals as Spain defeated Germany 3–0.

Last month she was awarded a record-equalling third Ballon d'Or.

Age: 29 Country: Jamaica

Club: Manchester City Position: Forward

After a fine year, Shaw has positioned herself as one of the world's elite forwards.

The defining striker in Manchester City's Women Super League title-winning campaign, she scored 21 goals in 22 league appearances, won a record third consecutive WSL Golden Boot and was named WSL Player of the Season.

Her goals were central to City ending a 10-year wait for the league title.

They went on to complete the Double, with Shaw scoring the opening goal in their FA Cup final victory over Brighton at Wembley to finish the season with 26 goals in all competitions.

She also reached a major personal milestone in December 2025 when she became the first player in the history of City's professional women's team to score 100 goals.

Amid uncertainty over her future, Shaw announced at City's end-of-season celebrations that she had signed a new four-year contract through to 2030.

Sports.title: Tiger Woods set for competitive golf return in December's Hero World Challenge
Sports.text:
Tiger Woods is set to return to competitive golf in December for the first time in more than two years.

Woods, 50, has not played in a traditional ranking event since the 2024 Open Championship at Royal Troon amid a series of off-course issues.

The 15-time major champion has endured a challenging few years with a number of injuries and turmoil in his personal life.

Woods will host next month's Hero World Challenge - an event which is part of the PGA Tour schedule but does not carry FedEx Cup points - and has been announced as part of the 20-player field.

The American is one of three exemptions for the tournament in the Bahamas along with compatriots Rickie Fowler and Gary Woodland.

Speaking to SiriusXM PGA Tour Radio in a video posted last week, Woods said: "I'm feeling better, no doubt about that.

"I've been training quite a bit. I will be at Hero either way, so I'll see you there."

Woods' long-awaited return comes after he accepted a five-year driving ban in September following a plea agreement in his reckless driving case.

In March, Woods had been arrested and charged with driving under the influence after clipping a truck and rolling his car in Florida.

Woods was also found with two white pills in his pocket, which were identified as hydrocodone - an opioid used to treat pain.

He subsequently stepped away from golf to seek treatment in what was described by his attorney as an "intensive, highly individualised and medically integrated programme".

Woods has endured a succession of debilitating injuries, including multiple back surgeries, serious fractures to his right leg following a car crash in 2021 and a ruptured Achilles tendon in 2025.

Woods also suffered the death of his mother, Kultida, in February 2025, while his girlfriend Vanessa Trump was diagnosed with breast cancer earlier this year.

Trump, the former daughter-in-law of US President Donald Trump, said last month that she is now cancer free.

Every report we had since Tiger Woods resurfaced into public life has told us he is looking good and looking fit. Going into the new year he will be taking part in his own indoor golf league, the TGL, so it's not the biggest surprise that he will be at his own tournament in the Bahamas.

This is the fifth time he has come back from a long-term absence from the game at this event. It is one that means an awful lot to him. It is involved with his charitable foundation and it's his tournament, so no surprise this is the one he has chosen to come back at.

The TGL in the new year, that's the indoor simulator run by his company in conjunction with Rory McIlroy. He did compete last year and cut a pretty pathetic figure by the standards of someone who has won 15 major titles. We could see him play before that at the PNC event. That's the parent and child event where he would presumably play with his son Charlie.

He is trying to line himself up to play at least the majors next year. They mean an awful lot to him.

We know how much the Masters means to him, but also think about where the US Open is going to be played, at Pebble Beach, and that's where he won the US Open in 2000 by 15 shots.

The Open Championship at St Andrews where he has won two of his three Open titles. These would be events he would certainly want to be at.

Sports.title: FA want to host Nations League finals in England
Sports.text:
England could host the Nations League finals this season after Football Association officials registered their interest.

The semi-final and finals of the competition, due to take place in June, are held in one country.

As well as England, it is understood that Spain and France have also contacted Uefa to register their interest in hosting the final four games, including the bronze medal match, which will run between 9-13 June.

The FA, it is understood, is still discussing potential venues with some doubt over whether Wembley would be available. The only publicly announced Wembley events in June are two concerts by singer Sam Fender, although these are for after the Nations League.

Since the tournament began in 2019, England have never held the finals, with Portugal, Italy, Netherlands and Germany the hosts to date.

Generally, only nations who reach the last four of the Nations League are considered to host the latter stages.

Thomas Tuchel's team will be seeded in Friday's draw for the quarter-finals following their euphoric 3-2 victory over Spain in Madrid, which secured top place in the group.

They could face Belgium, Netherlands, Denmark or Norway in March in the next round before June's finals.

If the FA's bid is successful, it will provide the governing body with an opportunity to host a mini-tournament before Euro 2028, which will be held in England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland.

Sports.title: London City forward Izzy Goodwin receives first England call-up
Sports.text:
London City Lionesses forward Izzy Goodwin has been named in the England squad for the first time for the World Cup qualifying play-off against Ukraine.

The 23-year-old has been in great form this month and scored in front of England manager Sarina Wiegman at Emirates Stadium on Sunday in a 1-1 draw with Arsenal.

"We have always seen her as a huge talent with potential," Wiegman told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"I think London City are developing really well in the games they have showed. She is tall and can head a ball attacking-wise, but also defending.

"She is really quick with her feet and can score goals. I really want to see her in our environment, what she can bring and how close she is to the level that we expect."

There is also a first call-up for goalkeeper Katie Cox, on loan at Nottingham Forest from Chelsea, while Manchester United midfielder Ella Toone returns.

Manchester City duo Niamh Charles and Alex Greenwood, who is injured, are among those to miss out.

The Lionesses play Ukraine in Spain on 1 December before hosting them at Wembley on 5 December. The winner qualifies for next year's Women's World Cup.

"We know what's at stake in these games and our focus is on producing two strong performances to secure our place at the World Cup," said Wiegman.

"We have worked hard to put ourselves in this position and now we have to finish the job.

"Ukraine will provide a challenge and we will prepare with the same focus and determination that we always do."

Chelsea defender Lucy Bronze could make her 150th appearance at Wembley in the second leg.

England travel to Pinatar, Spain a few days before the first leg and opted not to play a friendly match during this extended international break.

"The first part of the block we are [at St George's Park]. We have training sessions and a period of time where we can do some tactical stuff," added Wiegman.

"We also selected more players so that helps us create situations where we can train things and everyone is important. I'm really excited to get ready for these games."

Wiegman was speaking to media at St George's Park for the first time since signing a new contract that will run until the end of Euro 2029.

It means she could oversee England's fortunes at next year's World Cup if they beat Ukraine, as well as heading up a Team GB squad at the 2028 Olympic Games.

Asked why she wanted to extend her stay, Wiegman told BBC Radio 5 Live: "Well, first of all the FA is happy with me and I'm really happy with them.

"I'm really grateful for that environment. That is one [reason]. Secondly, I still feel a great connection with staff and players, and of course the country!

"Then we have the challenges ahead. The major tournaments always motivate me. You don't get many moments with the team because it's not like it is at a club.

"In a tournament, you have those moments where you are really together, you can get somewhere with the group and that really excites me.

"Yes, the Olympics would be really great. Next year it's the World Cup, then it's the Olympics, then it's the Euros – that journey ahead really excites me."

Wiegman's contract renewal was kept under wraps and it came as a surprise following their two-legged victory over Greece in October.

The Dutchwoman, who has guided England to successive European titles, said conversations had been ongoing for a while but she had not planned ahead.

"When I signed that first contract in 2020 to join in 2021, it was a four-year contract and I thought, 'ok, this is a long contract, it would be really great if things go well'.

"We all got so excited so I signed another contract until 2027 and now I have until 2029. That is eight years. I never expected that. I also never planned so far ahead.

"I want to feel that I can contribute to the environment and the development of things. I also want that from the other party. You want it to fit and for it to work.

"That decision came over time. At one point you think: 'Yeah, I'm getting really excited again.' That is what you want. To feel the energy, to feel the excitement.

"I still think we have things we can improve. We know the game is improving so quickly so we have to adapt all the time. When you stand still, you are lost."

Wiegman is also determined to improve as a coach and has enjoyed overseeing the development of younger talent as the Lionesses transition.

"It starts with me and about how I am going to develop. I keep learning things about myself too. You need to know yourself really well to do this job," she added.

"The staff and the players will always challenge me in the right ways. It goes back and forth. That is what I want. I really want to improve myself all the time."

Sports.title: A 2-0 win over Haiti ends Pochettino’s USMNT tenure with confident hope
Sports.text:
The US men’s national team is through to the semi-final of the Concacaf Nations League, following Saturday’s 6-0 romp with a workmanlike 2-0 win over Haiti in the Cincinnati-hosted second leg. Christian Pulisic opened the scoring with an acrobatic overhead goal, while 18-year-old Julian Hall scored his fifth goal in six caps since debuting in September. Towering 19-year-old center back Neil Pierre was cap-tied to the US with an appearance, eliminating the potential for him to represent Haiti in future windows.

In keeping a clean sheet, the United States has now played over 400 minutes without conceding a goal, last allowing a goal against Chile on 29 September.

The real impact of the match, though, is on the sideline; the win marks the end of the USMNT’s Mauricio Pochettino era, with the manager trading his summer safari duds for an all-black outfit including a puffer vest to mark his final match in the role. The Argentinian will now follow his assistants across the Atlantic to try turning things around at Manchester United. That undertaking will be even more daunting than the project he inherited from Gregg Berhalter two years ago, due to the scale of the work to be done and the relative expectations around United and the United States.

Much has been written, here and elsewhere, about the short-lived and abruptly ended Pochettino tenure. With his time in the role having firmly drifted into the rear-view, what can we make from his two-plus years in charge?

Pochettino and his staff launched a deep and wide-ranging survey of the US player pool in their first year, giving 77 different players run-outs over 25 months. That work didn’t just pull together a credible 26-man roster for the World Cup, but gave the group a crucial lens into the considerable rising talent this program boasts. By the time this international window rolled around, it wasn’t a surprise to see Hall, Diego Kochen, Cavan Sullivan, and other young emerging talents in the squad. The culture, in this game and across both of Pochettino’s final two windows, felt invigorated.

Indeed, while Pulisic’s acrobatic opener stunned, Julian Hall’s cool finish under pressure to double the lead in the 43rd minute might be the most promising sign of the US’s direction. The New York Red Bulls striker has exceptional ability to find space in the final third and a natural finishing touch, and after Saturday’s appearance is now cap-tied to the US after interest from Poland.

The US are now a near-blemishless 6-0-0 since getting bounced by Belgium in the last-16. The rout of Haiti will have hardly surprised, but the previous window saw the US completely outplay Mexico and withstand a physical test from Canada, as well as multi-goal wins over Chile and Peru.

“The way we played, that is what we dream[ed] when we arrived,” Pochettino told reporters afterward. “When you talk about these games, it looks like it was easy. But Haiti is a World Cup team. The players make the job easier.”

Then again, Pochettino’s tenure hasn’t seen players pushed beyond their comfort zones terribly often. Tuesday’s win in Cincinnati was the 35th of Pochettino’s 37 matches in charge to be played within the United States. The other two came nearby in Mexico and Jamaica.

International coaches seldom book their team’s friendlies, of course, and the global Nations League era makes booking cross-confederation dates a tough task. Still, it’s one that the federation would be wise to incorporate between now and a 2030 World Cup played across three continents. Haiti, for as heroic as their World Cup appearance was, were simply not on the same level as the US tonight or in Miami on Saturday, where the same US lineup played through them with ease.

At this stage, the US is largely composed of two bands of talent. The relative old guard is the wave ushered in by Pulisic at the tail-end of 2018 qualifying, with Tyler Adams, Weston McKennie, Antonee Robinson, and Chris Richards alongside, all between ages 26 and 29. Sullivan heads up the next generation, a group teeming with potential who grew up aspiring to follow in Pulisic’s footsteps. A few others, like Sebastian Berhalter, Folarin Balogun, Gio Reyna, Malik Tillman, and Alex Freeman bridge the gap. While there are still untapped options to test – with Santiago Castañeda and Reed Baker-Whiting becoming the 31st and 32nd national team debutants of Pochettino’s tenure on Tuesday – the skeleton is there upon which to flesh out a dark horse challenger for a deep World Cup run.

“I am sure that this group of players will achieve big things in the future. I have no doubt,” Pochettino said. “Experienced players, with the mix of younger talent that is coming, it’s the perfect combination.”

Pochettino also made clear that this player pool isn’t one to relish playing as relative underdogs. This is a generation of aspiring entertainers, players who want to dictate the proceedings by carrying a majority of possession and fashioning dangerous chances whenever on offer. How to sustain that ethos in the testy arenas of World Cup qualifying is now somebody else’s problem.

Along the way, Pochettino had a knack for heightening the national team’s relevance. Even on Tuesday afternoon, American sports programs like Pardon the Interruption that treat discussing soccer like a taboo that would demand censorship threw the US’s second leg against Haiti into the rundown.

The US men’s national team felt more important, because Pochettino decided it was important enough to lead it. Time will tell whether his successor can demand a similar focus.

Gaming_Tech.title: Critical flaw found in vital internet platform Java through AI
Gaming_Tech.text:
A cyber-security firm has used artificial intelligence (AI) to uncover a critical flaw in the hugely popular computer programming language Java.

Tech start-up Calif - which recently identified a cyber-security flaw in another language, PHP - found the bug in Java's memory functions.

Java is the world's third largest programming language used by 90% of the world's Fortune 500 companies like Apple and Amazon, and many banks, hospitals and governments.

The discovery comes after a string of serious technology issues, including a massive Microsoft outage and a network failure that grounded all US flights. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there is "zero evidence" the incidents are related.

More recently, the US National Security Agency said its internal communications went offline on Tuesday due to a "scheduled routine maintenance".

Apple also reported multiple services suffered full outages due to an internal update.

The NSA did not specify whether its outage was linked to the identified Java bug.

With the help of AI, Calif discovered a serious security vulnerability called Java4Shell, which allowed an adversary to remotely execute unwanted commands to Java's memory system.

That adversary was OpenAI's recently released model GPT-6 Cyber, which is not yet available to the public. But there are fears hackers could now identify the bug if the flaw isn't fixed.

Oracle, the owner of Java, has not acknowledged the bug, but released a "critical patch update" on Tuesday, which it said contained security vulnerability fixes. And at this stage it is unclear if any platforms or companies have been affected by the latest incident. The BBC has contacted Oracle for comment.

But the Java flaw remains a huge concern for cyber-security experts, who say overloading a system's memory is one of the most common ways for hackers to exploit or crash a system.

One of the main functions of Java is that it is supposed to manage and protect memory for you, Professor Toby Walsh, computer scientist and one of the world's leading researchers in AI, told the BBC.

"This is why this is such an unlikely and serious flaw," Walsh added. Java is meant to make the IT world more secure by managing your memory online, he said.

Anytime you transfer information on the internet, receive a file from a user or need to log into an IT system with a password, the platform you are using is likely relying on a Java program.

First released in 1995, the programming language and computing system is now the "beating heart of the modern economy", Calif said in its investigation.

Nearly every critical sector, including banking, national security systems, aviation and telecommunications, relies on Java.

It's a serious flaw that could comprise "critical financial systems, customers and organisation's data," cyber-security expert Dr Pedram Hayati said.

In Australia alone, almost every bank uses Java for managing critical transaction data, Hayati added.

As global security services or companies search for critical cyber-security flaws they are relying more on AI.

Earlier in November, OpenAI President Greg Brockman announced his company was pivoting 25% of its staff to focus on cyber-security demands.

The announcement followed a critical cyber-security flaw identified in the PHP programming language, identified by the same company Calif.

PHP is the code that websites like Wikipedia use to collect information and present it in a way you can read on the web.

Surrey Centre for Cyber Security Prof Alan Woodward said the PHP flaw affected some 30 million websites, leaving them vulnerable to malicious attacks.

At the time, website owners were urged to check if their sites were affected and, if so, they were told to install updates to patch the issue or consider going offline.

Earlier this week, thousands of customers at major US banks, including JP Morgan Chase, Wells Fargo and Bank of America, reported trouble accessing services.

The latest incidents have exposed how nearly every critical sector - including national security systems, aviation and telecommunications - rely on legacy infrastructure online.

The PHP flaws went undetected for at least a decade, which Walsh said is similar to what has happened with Java.

"It's been hiding in plain sight for 12 years", he said.

"AI is now exposing more flaws much more quickly," Walsh said including ones that may have been so obscure and difficult that humans could not have discovered them alone.

Gaming_Tech.title: Nvidia reports bumper results as firm says it's not reinstating Jensen Huang
Gaming_Tech.text:
Nvidia's quarterly sales doubled to top $100bn for the first time as the company insisted it has no plans to reinstate ousted co-founder Jensen Huang.

In the company's first results since Huang's dramatic exit, interim chief executive Colette Kress said it is "business as usual" and told investors: "We've got this."

The company's quarterly sales doubled from a year earlier, reaching $115.8bn (£86.9bn), with shares in the company jumping by 4.8% in after-hours trading.

Earlier on Tuesday, Huang said he would be "honoured" to return and lead Nvidia, having quit following alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected spy for China.

"The board does not intend to reinstate him," Nvidia chair Harvey Jones said during a call on Tuesday with financial analysts.

The company's profits also doubled from a year ago. For the quarter, which covered the three months to 25 October, profit hit $65bn. Its revenue from data centres, a significant part of Nvidia's business, also doubled to $107bn in the same period.

Going forward, the company said its rapid growth is poised to continue, and revenue will rise by another 13% in the next quarter.

Given the uncertainty surrounding the company after Huang's exit, financial analysts had been unsure that Nvidia would provide any forward-looking guidance.

Daniela Hathorn, a senior analyst for trading platform Capital.com, said Nvidia's results "offer a strong answer to concerns that demand for AI infrastructure is cooling" and temper immediate worries that Huang was irreplaceable as a leader.

"The harder question is whether Nvidia can preserve the strategic advantage Huang helped build," Hathorn added. "His exit is unlikely to change orders already committed, but could matter more when Nvidia makes its next round of decisions on products, partnerships and investment."

Kress seemed eager to stress that Nvidia can continue to not only succeed, but lead the ongoing AI buildout that is happening throughout the technology industry.

"It is business as usual," she said. "Our partners, our suppliers, all of them are 100% behind us."

She added that Nvidia's leadership team has "stood up very strongly over the last week... working seamlessly in all of their departments and projects".

"Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed." Kress said before leaving the analyst call. "We've got this."

The interim CEO also said Nvidia is no longer shipping Hopper data centre semiconductors to China.

The Hopper technology is in Nvidia's advanced H200 processors, which the firm won approval to sell in China after Huang's repeated lobbying efforts in Washington.

They had previously been restricted over concerns that selling them to China would give its industries and military an edge over the US.

Kress did not elaborate on why the shipments had been stopped.

Despite board chairman Jones saying earlier that the company would not answer analysts' questions about Huang or Nvidia's investigation into his conduct, he did address the search for a permanent replacement.

He said Nvidia is working with an executive search firm and is considering internal and external candidates, but that the company would not rush its selection.

"With the advanced technology and the national security dynamics in the marketplace, our new CEO will have to navigate those waters carefully," Jones said. "The search will be thorough and we want to do it as quickly as possible, but we won't do it before we find the exact right person."

Michael Monaghan from investment firm Founder ETFs is among those who want Huang back in the top job at Nvidia.

The Nvidia investor told the BBC that he is waiting to see the results of a thorough investigation into Huang's actions, instead of relying on "salacious allegations" made in the media.

Nvidia's strong earnings are "from the machine that Jensen built" and a company tends to lose "its shine and vision" after an iconic founder leaves, Monaghan said.

Gaming_Tech.title: How important is Jensen Huang to the US economy?
Gaming_Tech.text:
Nvidia and its co-founder Jensen Huang have been at the centre of the Artificial Intelligence (AI) spending boom.

No company or chief executive has arguably been more consequential to the development of AI in recent years, with the US microchip manufacturer under Huang positioning itself as a critical cog in the development of the world-changing technology.

That partnership has now ended following Huang's resignation over revelations of extramarital affairs, one of which is alleged to have been with a Chinese spy.

The company has been rocked by the scandal, with hundreds of billions of dollars wiped off its stock market value and questions swirling about the extent of the impact of Huang's departure.

While Nvidia is not as much of a household name as other Big Tech players such as Apple, Amazon and Microsoft, the company has been just as integral to the booming US stock market of recent years.

The billions of dollars being funnelled into AI and the construction of data centres has bolstered the American economy, with Nvidia being one of the biggest spenders.

Originally focusing on chips which process graphics for computer games, it pivoted to making the chips used in AI systems and now dominates the market.

It is now one the most valuable firms, worth $3.8 trillion (£2.9 trillion), and on Tuesday said its rapid growth is poised to continue as the firm's quarterly sales doubled from a year earlier.

But there's now an air of uncertainty over Nvidia's future direction. Huang played a major role in the company, leading its shift towards AI, and maintained a firm grip on the company, with up to 200 people directly reporting to him.

Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at investment firm AJ Bell, says because Huang was also a key figure in "flying the flag" to drum up enthusiasm and investment for the wider AI industry, his departure posed a "real risk" that Nvidia could now decide to change its current strategy and rein in spending.

Such a move could spell a wider slowdown in AI investment, which would have an economic impact. How big? That's "unknown", Coatsworth says.

"If they decide to go with the much more cautious route... there could be a knock-on effect in that you have got various companies in the AI infrastructure space suddenly finding they don't have a key source of finance," he says.

Kunjan Sobhani, senior technology industry analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence, expects the impact of Huang leaving to be "limited" for now as Nvidia has strong commitments and a deep order book. But he said this picture could change in the long run.

That is because Nvidia, on its journey to the top of the AI industry, has created a spider's web of deals through what is known as "circular financing".

Not only does it sell microchips to its customers, which include the likes of Meta, SpaceX and OpenAI, it has also provided funds for them and other firms in the supply chain by either handing out loans or investing in them directly.

The practice has prompted concerns among some investors, who worry what might happen if Nvidia were to turn off the spending taps. If investment dried up, would other firms in the supply chain cut spending or jobs themselves? Would that spread to the wider US economy?

That risk is perhaps why tech bosses including Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, the CEO of Fortnite maker Epic Games, have called for Huang's reinstatement.

Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation, which has also prompted a campaign by shareholders and supporters to "Bring Jensen Back".

Huang himself has said he is open to a return just after a week after resigning.

Coatsworth says he has never seen circular financing used at this scale before, but admits there are competitive rivals around, which could insulate the wider AI industry from any potential slowdown at the firm.

When Nvidia's share price plunged in the wake of the affair revelations, the stock of its rival semiconductor makers including AMD, Broadcom and Marvell Technology jumped.

"I don't think all AI activity grinds to a halt if Nvidia slows down what it's doing and if it pulls some financing, but it does change how people would look at the whole situation," Coatsworth adds.

Gaming_Tech.title: Nvidia: China fears Jensen Huang scandal could shut it out of US AI tech before Xi-Trump summit
Gaming_Tech.text:
Jensen Huang is out but his shadow looms over the upcoming meeting between US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping this week.

For Beijing, the former Nvidia CEO's dramatic fall is a major challenge - and not just because of claims that a Chinese spy may have honey-trapped Huang, one of the artificial intelligence industry's most influential figures.

Rather, the allegations surrounding Huang and his affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang are turning into a new flashpoint in an already fragile US-China relationship.

US intelligence reports claim she had ties to Beijing's intelligence apparatus - in particular the Ministry of State Security, China's main civilian spy agency.

The claim remains unproven, but it has already reignited debate in Washington over exports of advanced chips to China and whether the Trump administration has been too willing to ease restrictions.

For years now, advanced computer chips have been a key battleground in the US-China rivalry because they are essential for AI, supercomputing and military technology.

Chinese officials are worried this scandal could strengthen voices in Washington who argue in favour of further limiting Chinese access to cutting-edge American tech.

Just this week, the Trump administration introduced new export restrictions on Chinese firms that access advanced US chips in third countries such as Malaysia, Thailand or Brazil. They typically do this by renting computing power in data centres abroad to train their AI models. But some of the firms, like the one Alice Huang worked for, are also accused of smuggling chips to China, although they have denied this.

Until now, this controversy appeared to be a sideshow in US-China relations. But with Beijing calling the new rules "economic coercion" on the eve of Trump arriving in Shenzhen, there is a growing risk it could become something much bigger.

Democrats, who will control Congress come January, have made their position clear. Last Wednesday top Democrat Ted Lieu told Politico the Trump administration had been "1,000%" too deferential to Nvidia, putting national security at risk, while fellow Democrat Zoe Lofgren suggested Congress would now be more likely to restrict sales of AI chips to China.

The BBC has approached the White House for comment.

Beijing's foreign ministry had described the spy claims as a "smear against China".

"The US should stop fabricating so-called espionage narratives to find pretexts for imposing technological blockades," spokesperson Mao Ning said last week.

The ministry also seemed keen to keep the meeting on track, saying the two countries had kept "close communication regarding interactions between the two heads of state".

For the last year, Trump and Xi have been seeking to stabilise relations after a damaging tariff war that almost brought trade between the two countries to a standstill.

The Trump administration's decision to permit sales of advanced Nvidia H200 chips to China in late 2025 was seen as evidence that both sides were searching for areas of co-operation, even while competition intensified.

It was a rare move given Washington had spent years trying to limit China's access to the most advanced chips.

Many in the US have long viewed these chips as a national security issue, arguing they could strengthen China's military and surveillance capabilities. Jensen Huang, who rejects that claim, advocated lifting bans on the export of high-performing chips to China. Beijing argues the restrictions are an attempt to contain its rise.

Now that opening may be under threat.

History has taught Beijing and Washington that spy scandals rarely remain confined to the intelligence world.

Analysts in China already see echoes of an incident in 2023 when a suspected surveillance balloon drifted through the skies over the US before an American fighter jet shot it down. Beijing insisted it was a civilian meteorological airship that had strayed off course.

But a planned trip by then US Secretary of State Antony Blinken was cancelled and communication between the two governments deteriorated sharply.

The incident showed how quickly a security dispute could overwhelm diplomatic efforts and push relations into a deep freeze.

"The mere passage of a balloon sent American public opinion and politicians into a state of high alert, as if a "Chinese threat" were looming directly overhead," said the state media outlet, the Global Times this week as it made a direct comparison with the Nvidia scandal.

"No-one on the US side has ever apologised or taken responsibility for the genuine damage this caused to US-China relations," it added.

The state-run outlet also questioned why the Nvidia story had emerged so soon after "the hard-won detente" between Beijing and Washington, following a meeting between the two countries' leaders in September.

"Is someone behind the scenes pushing an agenda and stirring up confrontation?" it asked.

The summit is also being carefully choreographed by Beijing to show off its technological prowess in Shenzhen - a deeply symbolic choice of city.

It's home to some of the country's biggest tech companies and has become a showcase for Beijing's ambitions in AI and advanced manufacturing.

Also, given Washington's tighter restrictions on advanced chips, Beijing has options for retaliation.

One of its most powerful tools is its dominance of key rare earth minerals. China processes much of the world's supply for materials that are used in everything from electric vehicles and smartphones to military equipment.

Analysts have long warned that technological restrictions can trigger a cycle of retaliation in which each side reaches for its strongest economic leverage.

That would shift the current trend of US-China relations from engagement back towards mutual suspicion.

Gaming_Tech.title: Europe plans to catch the next computer chip wave
Gaming_Tech.text:
"Photonic chips are on the verge of a breakthrough," says Ton van Mol of the Dutch research institute TNO.

If van Mol is right – and TNO, the European Union and the Dutch government are backing the idea with millions of euros - then the technology could be a gamechanger.

The chips which run today's society, from your phone and TV, to the vast data centres meeting our insatiable desire for AI, are mostly electrical.

They process data by shunting electrons around tiny circuits – a single microchip produced today can contain billions of transistors, and sizes are measured in nanometres (one nanometre is a billionth of a metre).

Because they use light instead of electricity, photonic chips are faster, use less energy and generate less heat than traditional computer chips.

Van Mol hopes for an acceleration in photonics similar to the one seen in electrical chips since the 1970s.

"With optical chips, you are now where electronic chips were maybe 40 [or] 50 years ago."

American, Taiwanese and Chinese firms dominate the computer chip industry, but Europe sees the emergence of photonic chips as a fresh opportunity to lead, on what could be, a key future technology.

Which is why the European Union has committed €400m ($450m; £330m) to a project called PIX Europe, external, with the stated goal of making the continent "a global leader in emerging technology for Photonic Integrated Chips".

"Europe said 'we need to have our own manufacturing in-house'," says van Mol, who is leading a key part of the programme.

"We cannot depend like in the past that everything is manufactured in the US or China - that's not wise, so the [European] Chips Act was called into life, and one of the parts of the act is to build pilot lines to really bring the technology, which is now in labs, to the next stage - manufacturing."

Electronic and photonic chips are produced on wafers made up of hundreds of individual chips. Factories with machines that can handle bigger wafers can churn out chips more efficiently.

"[Photonic chip] manufacturing worldwide is [currently] done on wafers which are four inches (10cm) in size, and the next step is to scale-up production to a six-inch wafer," says van Mol.

His team are already building a 10,000 sq m factory to produce six-inch indium phosphide wafers on the High Tech Campus in the Dutch city of Eindhoven.

It's due to fully open in 2030 and will be a major step forward, not just for photonics in Europe, but around the world, according to van Mol.

"That's the development TNO is going to do, in a pilot line which is really serious.

"In 2030, we hope that we have a stable, reproducible, high-yield process, and then the intention is that the pilot line [opens] to industrial parties who can make commercial production out of it."

Europe does have one crucial player in the current computer chip industry - ASML.

The Netherlands-based tech giant is the only company in the world able to build the machines needed to make the most sophisticated semiconductors.

Which is why ASML products will sit at the heart of the pilot line in Eindhoven - it's no coincidence that van Mol's project is based around the corner from ASML's headquarters.

"The way you produce these [photonic] chips is very similar to the way you produce electrical or electronic chip," says van Mol.

"You use the same type of equipment, you also need a high-end clean room, you also use wafers, so the production method is very similar to the traditional semiconductor technology."

ASML itself is keen to explore the opportunities that the emerging technology of photonics could offer.

"Europe has a strong position in photonics research. The next challenge is translating those innovations into industrial-scale manufacturing," says Stanislas Baron, who is the head of ASML's EU/US Customer Team.

ASML's unique success has helped build an influential and lucrative network of companies and institutions devoted to semiconductor technology in and around Eindhoven, and it's a model for what Europe is trying to achieve with photonic chips.

The Eindhoven project has the backing of former ASML chief executive Peter Wennink, author of an influential report for the Dutch government called The Roadmap to Future Prosperity, external, which noted that the market for photonics was expected to grow 10 to 20 times in the next 10 years.

In a news release backing the new pilot line, Wennink described it as "a launchpad for Europe's future digital economy".

"By investing in scalable production capacity, we are creating an ecosystem that can help shape the global technological direction," he said.

Of course, Europe is not alone in looking to the potential of photonics to earn a global economic advantage.

In June this year, US photonics company Coherent, external announced what it called "the world's first and largest volume-production six-inch indium phosphide manufacturing platform" at its plant in Sherman, in Texas.

The expansion is backed by chip manufacturing giant Nvidia, as well as $50 million public funds under the US Chips Act.

It's an illustration of how quickly the market is moving, and how central photonic chips could be to the continuing race to retain an influential stake in AI and technological development more generally.

Europe's bid to establish itself as a global leader in photonic chips – exemplified by the Eindhoven project – is the kind of strategy that makes sense in a globalised economy, says Joris Teer, policy analyst at the European Institute for Security Studies in Brussels.

If the continent can take a lead in photonic chips, then future developments in AI and data will partly be dependent on Europe.

"Europe knows that its high energy and labour costs, skilled workforce shortages, and lack of private and public capital make an across-the-board reindustrialisation strategy impossible", Teer says.

"To retain influence, ensuring dependence on European parties rather than European autonomy is key."

Once up and running, the Eindhoven project will provide a pilot production line which can be used multiple companies.

It will be open to businesses across Europe and beyond, who can design and build chips without having to develop their own expensive production facilities.

"What we want to establish here is what we call a foundry model; there's no intention to have our own product," Ton van Mol says.

Instead, they will produce to order for outside customers.

It's the same idea which, at huge scale, has brought Taiwanese-based giant TSMC a position of global dominance in the manufacture of microchips.

Photonic chips are already in use, in highly specialised areas in data centres and in Lidar (light detection and ranging) sensor technology, for instance.

For van Mol of TNO, helping the industry to scale up, by easing production challenges and increasing capacity, is the key step to moving them into the tech we use in our daily lives, like phones and laptops, and to drive innovation in areas like medical scanners and 6G communications.

"The demand is there", says van Mol, "and the end goal is to have, in Europe, manufacturing of these chips, which is strategically very important because these chips [could] become the backbone of all data and telecom."

Gaming_Tech.title: Jensen Huang says he would be 'honoured' to return as Nvidia CEO if board asked him
Gaming_Tech.text:
Jensen Huang said he would be "honoured" to return as the boss of tech giant Nvidia if the board asked him to, in his first public comments since his shock resignation.

"I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely," Huang said on X, days after reports he had extramarital affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy.

He said he had an "outpouring" of calls from company employees, investors and others calling for him to return as CEO of Nvidia.

But, as the BBC reported on Monday, Nvidia's board is not considering bringing him back to lead the company.

The prospect of Huang returning at this point looks unlikely.

The company's board is investigating his conduct, which includes an alleged affair with an Nvidia executive.

The AI chip giant is set to report its financial results later on Tuesday, during which the company's interim chief executive, Collette Kress, may address the situation with Huang.

Beyond the internal Nvidia investigation, Huang's affair with a woman suspected of being an asset for Beijing is set to see the billionaire questioned before multiple committees of US lawmakers in the weeks ahead.

The Nvidia founder said he had "made serious mistakes in my personal life".

Nonetheless, Huang's statement appeared to show some hope he would be able to move past the major corporate scandal.

Huang said people have continued to "reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics".

"If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honoured to answer these calls and return as CEO," Huang added.

Many technology executives in recent days have praised Huang's role in the artificial intelligence boom. A petition began circulating online over the weekend calling for his reinstatement at the company.

Yet, by Monday, many executives were not openly calling for Huang's return.

Brad Gerstner, a major tech investor who knows Huang personally and also holds a significant stake in Nvidia, last week wrote an open letter saying that Nvidia could consider Huang's reinstatement.

On Monday, Gerstner said during an event hosted by Semafor that his letter had been misunderstood and the investigation into Huang's conduct needed to run its course.

While Gerstner questioned the facts around Huang's departure, he added: "I don't know to what degree he misled the board. If I was on a board I would take that very seriously. Let's be clear no one is above the law."

Gaming_Tech.title: How Trump's chip restrictions on South East Asia will hit China
Gaming_Tech.text:
As US President Donald Trump heads to China, his administration has renewed efforts to curb Beijing's access to advanced semiconductors.

On Monday, Washington announced new interim rules that will increase scrutiny of data centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil.

The move not only restricts the export of advanced chips, but also access to their computing power, which Chinese firms currently rent abroad to train artificial intelligence (AI) models.

South East Asian countries in particular have invested heavily in data centres to power their AI ambitions - and Chinese firms seeking computing power overseas have been a key market.

But now these firms will need a US government licence to buy advanced chips from Nvidia or other American chipmakers. This allows Washington to monitor if those chips are being used to serve Chinese companies, or being smuggled to China.

This poses a fresh challenge for Beijing, which has become deeply dependent on compute from abroad in the wake of US export restrictions. At least 30% of China's advanced AI computing power is projected to come from renting overseas or smuggling in 2027, according to research by the Institute for Progress, external, a US-based think-tank.

China's foreign ministry called the new rules "economic coercion" and said Beijing "will take necessary measures to firmly safeguard its own legitimate rights and interests".

This is also a problem for South East Asian economies where large numbers of data centres have sprung up recently. Some of the firms behind them are accused of helping China evade US export controls on advanced chips.

One of those is Singaporean data centre firm Megaspeed, whose former director Alice Huang is suspected of being a Chinese spy. Calls for tighter export controls have grown after Nvidia's Jensen Huang admited to an affair with her and resigned as CEO.

Megaspeed, the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in South East Asia, is accused of illegally smuggling chips to Chinese companies after purchasing them for use in data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.

The company has denied these allegations, defended its business as "legitimate and lawful", and said it has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation". It also said Alice Huang stepped down from her role as director in late 2023 and left the firm last year.

The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, however, has said Brazil and the four South East Asian nations "present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion" of the chips that Washington wants to keep out of China's hands.

The new measures are aimed at ensuring sensitive US technology "cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the bureau added. Licences will be issued on a "case-by-case basis", it said.

Countries like Malaysia and Thailand whose data centre roll out has been heavily driven by Chinese buyers could be hit hardest, says international trade expert Naoise McDonagh from Australia's Edith Cowan University.

But the new rules are unlikely to derail the data centre boom as a whole, says Reema Bhattacharya from advisory firm Verisk Maplecroft, adding that investment backed by major tech firms and clearly identifiable customers should "remain relatively resilient".

Singapore was an early adopter of data centres but when it began limiting new construction, investment flowed to neighbours Malaysia and Thailand. Johor in Malaysia and Batam in Indonesia have also approved billions of dollars worth of data centres to catch the spillover demand.

These countries have been offering incentives such as cheaper land to attract foreign investment, including from Chinese tech giants Alibaba and Tencent.

But now, the region could find it harder to get hold of advanced chips.

The BBC has contacted Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand for comment.

Singapore said it is "engaging relevant US authorities" to understand the new rules better, and is "exploring how to facilitate trusted access" for local firms.

A spokesperson for Brazil's Ministry of Development, Industry, Trade and Services said it is aware of the US announcement and it "is closely monitoring any potential developments regarding this measure".

Malaysia previously said it welcomes data centre investment but "will not allow itself to be used to get around export controls".
