Gaming_Tech.title: NHS data contract to stay with controversial US tech giant Palantir until 2029
Gaming_Tech.text:
The government says it will continue a key NHS data contract in England with the controversial US tech giant Palantir until 2029, rather than triggering an early release clause next year.

But ministers are inviting British firms to bid for the contract from 2029, with a procurement programme beginning next summer.

A Commons Committee had called on the government to part ways and appoint a company "more compatible with UK values". Protesters regularly target Palantir over Israel's use of its technology in the Gaza conflict and oppose its use in US immigration enforcement.

The £330m deal, which began in 2024 to help manage hospital waiting lists in England, was due to run until 2031.

The prime minister had faced pressure from some Labour MPs to cut ties with Palantir. They said they were extremely disappointed by the decision, calling the contract "an albatross" hanging around the NHS's neck.

The Liberal Democrats said the deal was "dangerous".

There have also been concerns raised about how patient data will be used.

Palantir, which was co-founded by billionaire Peter Thiel, has interests in US defence and security, and has contracts with the Israeli military.

Health minister James Frith said the move was "not about the politics of executives of suppliers, nor is it about the territories or customers that one company or one supplier makes".

The government says UK companies will be encouraged to tender to avoid overdependence on one supplier.

The timeframe is not fast enough for some members of the government.

Dame Chi Onwurah, Labour MP for Newcastle upon Tyne Central and West, said the government needed to "act urgently" to procure "credible domestic alternatives".

"The government should not wait two years, it must start reducing this dependency now," she said.

Former Labour shadow chancellor John McDonnell went further, and accused Palantir of "human rights abuses". He said his constituents in Hayes and Harlington "expect the contract to be ended".

Liberal Democrat health spokeswoman Helen Morgan criticised the company for what she called its "appalling human rights record, run by an ally of Donald Trump".

The British Medical Association, which represents doctors, said it was glad the government had shown it was listening to its concerns about Palantir, but was frustrated the process of changing to another company was further delayed.

Palantir UK said it was right to press forward with the programme which was exceeding targets.

"We are proud of our work to date to help deliver more operations, speed up discharge and reduce the time patients need to wait to find out if they have cancer," Palantir UK senior vice-president Tom Watson said.

Gaming_Tech.title: New Zealand tricks and annual leave - the lengths fans are going to for GTA 6
Gaming_Tech.text:
Grand Theft Auto fans have waited 13 long years for the latest edition of the game to be released - and going to extreme lengths to be ready for its launch.

GTA 6 will be released at midnight on Thursday - and Victoria Evans, from West Sussex, is not leaving anything to chance.

She has her alarm set for 05:00 GMT, and has a day off booked. She says she put the game's release on her leave request form which was approved, she told BBC News, despite the fact her boss "doesn't know what GTA 6 is".

She's far from the only one. For the game's launch day, HR software company BrightHR, external looked at absence data from more than 1.2 million employees from 70,000 businesses across the UK.

It found GTA was mentioned in 4.6% of time-off requests by employees. Throughout November and December, it said an estimated 83,000 days had been booked off for the game.

And booking leave is only one of the ways fans are making sure for the big day. Others are buying a new console to play it on or even pretending they're halfway around the world to get early access.

Some places have decided to lean into the trend for GTA 6 by offering incentives around the game - including the US Army's 3rd Infantry Division based at Fort Stewart, Georgia.

It gave some active-duty soldiers a four-day pass to play the game when it is released in November, as long as they sign a reenlistment contract for a minimum of two years between 1 August and 12 November.

"The idea was to have a unique incentives programme that connects to what soldiers are interested in," public affairs officer for the division, Lieutenant Colonel Angel Tomko confirmed to the BBC in August.

"There are 130 soldiers eligible within the battalion, and 20 have selected this incentive as part of their reenlistment," she said at the time.

Aside from taking time off, some gamers have also been discussing a technical loophole which could give them valuable extra hours of play before it officially unlocks in their country.

Because GTA 6 will release at midnight local time in all regions, New Zealand will become one of the first places where it is available, due to it reaching midnight earliest because of its position near the international date line.

This has led to some investigating ways to "trick" their consoles into thinking they're based in the island country when they are in fact thousands of miles away.

According to Google Trends, searches for the "GTA 6 New Zealand trick" have surged by more than 5,000% in the UK over the past month.

Games journalist Vic Hood said many gamers would be looking to play earlier to "get in on the action as soon as possible", as well as to prevent spoilers.

"As New Zealand is 13 hours ahead of the UK, that's 13 hours of gameplay that has time to spread across the internet and potentially spoil some key story beats and in-game surprises," she said.

"Took an extra day of paid time off when I found this out," one fan posted on Reddit on the trick.

It also means gamers would be playing the game at the much nicer time of 11:00 GMT, rather than having to stay up all night.

But another Xbox user shared caution on Reddit, noting that while the loophole had been exploited for many years for other game releases, GTA 6 "might be the game where Microsoft finally does something about this 'exploit'" - which could include banning players.

GTA 6's developers Rockstar and publishers Take Two Interactive have not commented on the loophole, and neither have Sony nor Microsoft.

Louise Wooldridge from Ampere Analysis said both Microsoft and Sony had "rules governing regional accounts and purchases" for the Xbox and PlayStation, adding that Sony's were "slightly more restrictive".

Players who choose to use the workaround could therefore risk breaching those terms and conditions and potentially face restrictions on their accounts or lose access to their digital games.

Some gamers will have to wait even longer than their console-playing counterparts to get their hands on GTA 6, as the game will not be available on PC at launch, similar to previous GTA releases.

"Spare a thought for the PC users who will have to live vicariously through others' YouTube videos and Twitch streams," gamer Stephen Finn told the BBC.

A PS5 now costs from £520, while the more powerful PS5 Pro is nearly £790.

Despite the hefty price tag, for some the temptation to join the community in playing what many have called the biggest game launch of the year, if not decade, has been too great.

Reddit posts and videos, such as one by US YouTuber isoish, external, show fans buying consoles specifically to play the game.

"So, the only game I'm going to have on here is GTA," the content creator said in the video.

"The whole PS5 is for GTA 6."

After more than a decade of waiting, it seems some fans are determined not to waste a single minute of GTA 6's release - no matter the cost or extra effort.

Additional reporting: Kris Bramwell

Gaming_Tech.title: US government confirms investigation into tech firm Megaspeed
Gaming_Tech.text:
The United States has confirmed it is investigating computing company Megaspeed, suspecting it of violating US export controls by helping to ship tech giant Nvidia's chips to China.

In a joint statement, the US Department of Justice and Department of Commerce said they had been investigating Singapore-based firm Megaspeed since 2024.

It comes after questions were raised about the possibility high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.

Concerns emerged in recent weeks after Nvidia founder Jensen Huang revealed he had an extramarital affair, allegedly with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang. US authorities suspect her of spying for Beijing, which China denies.

Jensen Huang resigned from his role as chief executive last week following revelations he had two affairs.

Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in South East Asia and is suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China. The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.

The justice and commerce departments said on Monday that "it is in the public interest to provide the facts and address inaccurate information" regarding the investigation.

Laying out a timeline, it said it began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations".

In May 2025, Department of Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia "concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed". In June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its 'no sell' list.

Agents from the Bureau of Industry and Security, in conjunction with Singaporean law enforcement officials, then conducted an on-site check at Megaspeed that month and interviewed Alice Huang, who was chief executive at the time.

Gaming_Tech.title: 'We're a capitalist society': Grindr defends $120 a month premium tier
Gaming_Tech.text:
The world's largest LGBTQ+ dating app, Grindr, has defended its $120 (£91) per month premium subscription service, which launches globally today.

Edge offers AI-powered services such as daily personalised profile recommendations that aim to provide better matches and limit scrolling.

The company's CEO, George Arison, told BBC News it would be a "very different Grindr experience" which was aimed at a "small community of users" - and was unapologetic about its cost.

"I think we're a capitalist society, and everything hinges on whether you can afford it or not," he said.

Grindr has long had a free service, and offers two additional tiers that cost between $22.99 and $44.99 per month.

There was a mixed reaction from users BBC News spoke to in San Francisco to the new, more expensive version of the app.

"The current premium Grindr tier is already really expensive," said one user who told the BBC the company's newest offering "just seems really out of touch with the community."

"I think that that's really disheartening, and it kind of leaves a bad taste in my mouth," added another user, Adrian, who declined to give his last name.

"The cost doesn't bother me," said a user named Michael. "All of these apps have premium tiers so saying that Grindr shouldn't have that when like it exists across all these other apps used for connection doesn't make sense."

He noted that high-end dating apps like The League can charge much more.

Grindr has been experimenting with Edge for much of the last year in markets including the US, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand.

On its earnings call earlier this month, the company said almost 400,000 users had registered for the service in the first 72 hours that it was available for testing.

Inside Grindr, Edge is viewed as a way to drive future growth in an industry has struggled in recent years.

For those who can afford it, the service promises to offer insights about a user's compatibility with prospective matches. It also resurfaces a user's past connections alongside summaries of previous interactions.

The current $120 monthly fee comes after the company tested charging hundreds of dollars more than that. And Arison has left open the possibility of increasing the cost in the future.

Arison told the BBC he's not concerned that intoducing an ultra-premium offering will pit "haves" against "have-nots" on the social networking platform.

Edge users "being willing to pay more for that set of features will result in us being able to subsidise the product for everybody else," Arison said.

"It's a choice that people make on whether they want to be on it."

Gaming_Tech.title: Nvidia dismisses campaign to bring back Jensen Huang as Trump backs effort
Gaming_Tech.text:
Nvidia has dismissed a campaign calling for the company's co-founder Jensen Huang to be handed back his job as allies, including US President Donald Trump, supported the effort.

Trump said on Monday that he "would certainly not mind" if Huang was reinstated, joining a list of supporters including SpaceX's Elon Musk who are backing a "Bring Jensen Back" campaign.

But the BBC has been told the board of the AI chip giant is not interested in reinstating him after he resigned last week following revelations he had two affairs, including one that involved a suspected Chinese spy.

The same day, the White House also said it will further restrict China's access to AI chips from firms like Nvidia.

The reported affairs created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms - a central company in AI and the US battle against China for dominance.

Since Huang's departure, more than 175,000 people have signed an open letter calling for the board to reinstate the tech billionaire while an ongoing internal probe is conducted.

Major tech bosses, including Musk and Tim Sweeney, chief executive of Fortnite-maker Epic Games, have also supported Huang's return.

The "Stand with Jensen" campaign claims to have been launched by current and former Nvidia employees, partners, shareholders and supporters, all demanding the return of the former chief executive.

They expressed concerns the firm's co-founder "was removed without meaningful due process".

Trump gave his views on Huang's future on Monday, saying he "would certainly not mind" seeing the former boss given his job back.

Huang had been expected to weather the storm following the revelation of the affair but resigned last Thursday after a second extra-marital relationship emerged, allegedly with an executive at Nvidia who reported to him.

The scandal-hit tech boss was discussing a possible return to Nvidia with confidants, according to the Financial Times, external, though Nvidia's board is not considering reappointing him.

A representative for Huang declined to comment on the report.

The so-called war room also wants to get support for Huang from the White House.

Trump has spoken in glowing terms about Huang since the scandal erupted, and also said he believed Huang when the former Nvidia boss told him he had "no idea she was a spy".

Trump's view is at odds with his Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who has called for Nvidia to hire its next chief executive from outside the company.

The scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end Nvidia chips to Alice Huang's former firm, Megaspeed. China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy.

It has raised questions about the possibility that the chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.

The Trump administration on Monday also issued new restrictions on chip exports to overseas data centres, which have been allegedly used as a way for Chinese firms to gain access to advanced chips to train AI models.

The move comes ahead of a meeting this week between Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping, whose countries are locked in a race to lead AI development.

The interim rules will require companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to apply for export licences for the most advanced chips in an effort to prevent them from being illegally diverted to China.

The measure is designed to ensure existing restrictions on sensitive US technology "cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the Department of Commerce said.

Huang has been a vocal advocate for easing chip export restrictions on China, arguing that broad access to global markets is crucial for the competitiveness of the US.

He said in 2025 that the market for AI chips in China would eventually reach $50bn - a sum Huang said "is like Boeing - not a plane - the entire company".

In 2025, Nvidia won an approval to sell some advanced AI chips in China after Huang's repeated lobbying efforts in Washington.

The ex-Nvidia boss' affair with Alice Huang, the former director of a Singaporean data centre firm called Megaspeed, has raised the level of scrutiny over deals abroad.

The small South East Asian business hub has been a draw for companies all around the world, many of which have set up headquarters in Singapore.

Major US firms like Anthropic, OpenAI and Google have set up offices in the business-friendly country, alongside Chinese companies like TikTok-owner ByteDance and Tencent.

But Singapore's openness to business has also made it the ideal address to place orders for restricted advanced semiconductors.

Singapore was the second-largest billing centre globally last year for Nvidia, accounting for nearly a fifth of what the chip giant earns.

But notably, only 2% of its earnings were for chips that actually entered Singapore, which acts as a hub for many Asian companies to place orders and send them elsewhere.

Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation.

"Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract," he posted on X., external

"Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost."

Fellow tech boss Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, sidestepped the question of Huang returning to Nvidia at a conference, saying: "I don't think I know enough to answer that question."

But Altman, who himself was reinstated to his job after being fired back in 2023, said Huang was a "hero of mine".

Shareholders in Nvidia also want Huang back at the company's helm.

Hundreds of billions of pounds have been wiped off the firm's stock market value in recent days, but it is still worth some $3.87 trillion. Its share price was down in early Monday trading.

In an open letter to the board, Brad Gerstner, founder of Altimeter Capital and Atreides Management boss Gavin Baker called for management to leave "all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang".

Lord Sarfraz, a member of the UK's House of Lords, has also written to Nvidia's new chair, Harvey Jones, urging the firm's directors to give "serious consideration" to Huang's return following the investigation.

For the moment, Nvidia's chief financial officer Colette Kress is leading the firm and will present the company's results on Tuesday.

Entertainment.title: Jeff Bezos was 'heavily involved' in Robert Pattinson's casting as Bond
Entertainment.text:
Jeff Bezos has said he was "heavily involved" in casting Robert Pattinson as the new James Bond.

Speaking at an event in California, the Amazon CEO said he was originally "biased against" Pattinson - who starred in many blockbuster films like Batman and the Twilight series - "because he's already so famous".

The role of 007 has typically gone to an actor who is not as well-known at the time of casting. But Bezos said in screen tests, "it was so obvious he is James Bond".

This will be the first 007 not under the creative control of the Broccoli family, who had overseen the franchise since the first Bond film in 1962. Amazon purchased MGM, which co-owns the franchise, in 2022.

"There was something special about Rob", Bezos said at Semafor Silicon Valley & The World Event on Tuesday.

Pattinson was unveiled as the franchise's seventh James Bond on Monday, taking over from actor Daniel Craig. He will star in the 26th Bond movie, due to be released in 2028.

In a statement, the London-born actor said: "James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime."

The next Bond film will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, but its title and exact release date have not yet been announced.

The announcement comes after years of intense speculation about who will take over from Craig in one of the most high-profile - and highly scrutinised - roles in entertainment.

Several other actors, including Josh O'Connor, Callum Turner and Jack Lowden, were reported to be in the frame for the role as screen tests took place in recent weeks.

But Amazon MGM ultimately went with a household name, choosing a more bankable movie star who is widely seen as a safe pair of hands.

"We ran a really tight process and made the final decision on Friday," Bezos said.

There were five finalists who went through "real, old-fashioned screen tests", acting out three different scenes in full costume, with real sets and other actors, he said.

"By the time we got to this list of five, they were all amazing. But there was something special about Rob and his performance," Bezos added. "It was immediately un-debated. Denis [Villeneuve], the director … we all gravitated toward Rob."

The pick comes amid widespread Hollywood cuts and consolidation, with studios struggling to get people into cinemas.

Hollywood insiders have said Pattinson was viewed as a safe pick to bring audiences in, rather than taking a risk on a new actor who could grow with the franchise.

"Maybe he's boring. Maybe Hollywood would be passing up a chance to anoint a badly needed new star. But with so much at stake for everyone involved, that all makes him the obvious pick," Hollywood journalist Matthew Belloni, who predicted the pick, wrote in his newsletter.

The BBC's Regan Morris contributed to this report.

Entertainment.title: Batman to James Bond: The clues about what to expect from Robert Pattinson's 007
Entertainment.text:
He has been in big-budget blockbusters like Twilight, Tenet and The Batman, as well as a string of quirky arthouse films - so what clues can Robert Pattinson's past roles give us about what he might be like as James Bond?

Every actor creates a new James Bond, and Pattinson is one of the best in the business at crafting a memorable character.

The British actor can be an action man or an anti-hero, a romantic lead or a comic fool. He can be granite-faced or goofy, and everything in between.

"I was thinking about what the aspects of James Bond are, and he's done all of those throughout his career," says Paul Tweddle, host of the Heavy Spoilers film podcast, external.

He cites Pattinson's performance as a brooding heartthrob in teen vampire franchise Twilight, his suave and quick-witted secret agent in Christopher Nolan's Tenet, the withdrawn and focused title character in The Batman, and the ruthless and manipulative Antinous in Nolan's The Odyssey.

Pattinson has "often been drawn to really dark fare", says Anna Smith, film critic and host of the Girls on Film podcast, external.

"Wouldn't it be interesting to see Bond go a little bit darker?" she suggested to the BBC's World Service. "But also what he's got, and I'd like him to do more of, is comedy. And goodness knows, we need a Bond who can handle humour."

Unusually for a James Bond actor, one word that has cropped up frequently is "weird".

Earlier this month, Pattinson was described as "the weirdest guy in Hollywood" by the Celebrating Cinema podcast, external.

"Pattinson is an actor who makes bold, interesting, risky choices. For such a handsome guy, he can bring the weird, and then some," wrote Chris Hewitt in Empire, external.

"About 0.07 seconds after the announcement, people were already anticipating the weird with his Bond. And they may well get their wish."

Variety's chief critic Guy Lodge said, external Pattinson's reputation as an actor "has been considerably enriched by his predilection for playing, frankly, losers and weirdos", such as in more offbeat films like Good Time, The Lighthouse, Primetime and Mickey 17.

"Even his blockbuster assignments are more interesting when he lets his inner freak out to play," Lodge added. "His big, heightened, leeringly villainous turn in The Odyssey is off on its own beam entirely."

Associated Press film critic Jake Coyle said, external smaller films like The Lighthouse and High Life show "Pattinson's proclivity for pushing boundaries".

"He's certainly the funniest and quickest to laugh James Bond we've had in decades," Coyle continued. "It will be interesting to see how much of his personality bleeds into Bond, or how much the tux stifles it."

Pattinson plays a dapper and enigmatic British agent in Christopher Nolan's time-bending 2020 thriller, as adept at bungeeing off an arms dealer's tower as he is delivering some deliciously dry wit.

"He's very suave, he's thinking on his feet," Tweddle says. "He's someone who's holding his cards close to his chest and not necessarily giving the game away.

"Tenet is the obvious one where Nolan's basically doing a kind of James Bond movie."

The Times' chief critic Kevin Maher agrees, external: "Pattinson has effectively played Bond already, when he effortlessly inhabited the role of the suave yet nonetheless lethal British spy Neil in Tenet.

"For many observers (including this one) that was the role. That was the audition. There was no turning back after Neil."

New York Times critic Alissa Wilkinson noted that Pattinson has picked up other "Bond-adjacent" roles. "The most obvious is Bruce Wayne, a.k.a. Batman, the wealthy playboy with a lair of tech toys and his own gussied-up automobile," she wrote, external.

"Wayne and Bond have a lot in common on paper, but in Pattinson's hands Wayne becomes emo, reclusive, awkward, with the hair of a '90s grunge rocker."

The Guardian's Peter Bradshaw also pointed out, external parallels with how Pattinson played "the darkly conflicted caped crusader Batman in Matt Reeves's 2022 film, lurking athletically in the shadows - like Bond, used to working in secret".

Like Tenet, The Batman proved Pattinson is an expert at action scenes, whether that be jumping off a building or being involved in an explosive car chase with The Penguin.

"Batman is a really good example of where he's a withdrawn figure, someone who has his mind focused solely on a task, and I think that's a big part of what James Bond needs to be," Tweddle says.

However, Pattinson's 007 should be a little less brooding and aloof than his stony-faced Batman and Bruce Wayne.

Although Pattinson plays the villain in Nolan's Greek epic, Antinous's menace and ruthlessness could come in handy when playing Bond, according to Tweddle.

"I think Robert Pattinson also has quite a psychotic side to him, which a lot of the James Bond books delve into - how he's a killer, and he needs to have that side to him," he says.

"What he's done in The Odyssey shows he can be manipulative, and connive and make certain plans, which is what a spy needs to do."

Collider's Collier Jennings named, external The Odyssey, along with Tenet and The Batman, as films that show Pattinson is "the perfect" fit for Bond.

"All three roles carry an element that makes James Bond work," Jennings wrote.

"Batman has the combat skills and subterfuge you'd need to be a spy of Bond's caliber, not to mention the cutting edge hardware.

"Neil has a great grasp on the intricacies of pulling off complex covert operations.

"Antonius walks with a swagger and arrogance that either makes you love him or hate him."

Pattinson will next be seen playing shape-shifting villain Scytale in the forthcoming third instalment of the epic sci-fi series - directed by Denis Villeneuve.

The pair's reunion for the next Bond movie is not a coincidence. Villeneuve's experience of working with Pattinson on the film may have been the deciding factor when casting James Bond.

"The thing I adore with Robert Pattinson is that when you roll cameras, there's always a certain moment where you have no idea what will happen. He is an explosion in front of the camera," the director told Time, external before the Bond casting was announced.

"He has an incredible imagination and is a very playful actor, and a very creative actor, always trying to bring new ways of expressing himself and always trying to surprise me."

Surprising, bold, weird? One thing is for certain, Pattinson's James Bond is going to be interesting.

Entertainment.title: Channel 4 admits it doesn't know number of Married At First Sight UK sex abuse complaints
Entertainment.text:
Channel 4's chief executive has admitted she doesn't know how many complaints of sexual misconduct were received about Married at First Sight UK, despite a six-month external review into the hit TV show.

When asked by MPs, Priya Dogra said: "I'm not sure I have the details," adding that the review looked specifically at the claims of three women featured in a BBC Panorama.

Married at First Sight UK was cancelled after Panorama revealed rape allegations from two female cast members, while a third woman alleged a non-consensual sex act. The men involved have denied all the allegations.

Separately, Dogra said the broadcaster "cannot apologise enough" to a former employee who twice made complaints about Russell Brand and felt they weren't properly handled.

Dogra said it was "almost unforgivable" that the woman said she complained to Channel 4 in 2009 and again in 2023.

Brand is serving a 10-and-half-year prison sentence after recently being found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

Married at First Sight UK, known as MAFS UK, had been running for 10 seasons and was one of Channel 4's biggest shows, with audience figures often topping three million.

The Panorama investigation in May heard from three women who made allegations about the men they were partnered with - claims the men deny:

One woman said her on-screen husband raped her and threatened her with an acid attack.

A second woman told both Channel 4 and production company CPL, before broadcast, about being allegedly raped by her on-screen husband. Her episodes were still aired.

A third woman accused her on-screen husband of sexual misconduct.

All three women accused the show of not doing enough to protect them.

A review was commissioned into MAFS UK by Channel 4 shortly after the BBC first contacted the broadcaster with details of the allegations.

Earlier this month, the completed review recommended extra safeguards on the show. But Channel 4 said the programme had "run its course" and apologised to the women involved in the investigation.

Speaking to MPs on the House of Commons culture and media committee on Tuesday, Dogra was repeatedly asked if she knew how many allegations Channel 4 and CPL had received over the years that MAFS UK was on air.

"I looked specifically into those instances [the three women], I did not do a broad sweep of every episode or every season of the show. That is not what the terms of reference for the show were," she responded.

"If there are others, we would take them seriously and look into them on the same basis."

"You're saying your inquiry didn't actually look at how many complaints were made into this show in total?" replied the committee's chair, Dame Caroline Dinenage.

"The inquiry looked at our handling of these specific incidents," responded Dogra.

When pushed about who would know how many allegations of harm had been received over the years, Dogra said that information would be held internally between Channel 4 and CPL.

Dogra, who started as Channel 4 chief executive earlier this year, also said she was "frankly uncomfortable" with some of the changes proposed by the review into MAFS UK - such as 24-hour CCTV and lockable bedrooms - hence her reason for axing the show.

Channel 4's bosses were also questioned at length about Brand by MPs in the hearing.

Brand's work on Channel 4 included hosting Big Brother sister show Big Brother's Big Mouth and its celebrity equivalent from 2004 to 2007, a chat show in 2006, and appearing on Big Fat Quiz of the Year.

Addressing Dogra and Channel 4's chairman Geoff Cooper, MPs said the member of staff who made two complaints about Brand "fell through the cracks".

In response, Dogra said: "I'm not sure we can apologise enough as an organisation for putting her through that twice. We have apologised in public in the past and in private."

She accepted that the woman's complaints were "not handled properly" and added that "it's almost unforgivable that happened twice".

When asked by the committee if junior members of staff could raise complaints against a star without fear of losing their job, Dogra replied she "can't say 100%" that that would be the case.

"What I can do is set the standard, set the tone, make sure that the facilities are available, make sure that my staff and the production companies understand the repercussions of not complying, and understand the kind of culture that I'm trying to set, and we're trying to set as an industry."

She also said she found the "cultural personality" around Brand "horrendous".

"I find it distasteful, and I look at the jokes... that is the lowest form of humour, because these are jokes that are made at the expense of someone else's physical safety.

"I don't believe it should have been acceptable then, and I certainly don't think it's acceptable now."

During the session, Dame Caroline also put to Channel 4 bosses that in both the MAFS UK and Brand cases, the broadcaster appeared like "a child with their hand in the cookie jar".

The committee chairwoman asked: "To what extent can you reassure us that Channel 4's priority is genuinely the welfare of the staff who work there, the staff who have worked there, and the people who take part in your shows - rather than purely when the world is looking at you and you suddenly feel that you've got a reputational reason to take a look at these shows?"

Dogra responded by saying that when Channel 4 commissioned the review, "we didn't even know whether the Panorama programme would be made".

She added: "We had received a right-to-reply letter and the programme came out six weeks later, but it equally it could not have been made. We always intended to do the review."

In the instance of the woman who tried to complain about Brand, she added: "I'm not sure there are more apologies we can give. Because none of those things should've happened."

Entertainment.title: Hunger Games prequel splits opinion: 'Surreally awful' or 'surprisingly strong'
Entertainment.text:
Reviews of the latest Hunger Games film have seen it dismissed as a "surreally awful prequel" and "a tortuous, costly mess" by some critics - but called "surprisingly strong" and "one of the best films in the series" by others.

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is the sixth movie in the franchise, and tells the origin story of a teenage Haymitch Abernathy - who was played as an adult by Woody Harrelson.

In a one-star review, the Guardian called the film, external "overwrought and boring", and said it "has no actual interest and no authentic reason to exist, other than to gouge an income stream out of its fanbase".

But the Wrap praised its, external "memorable performances, intoxicating style and horrifying commentary", adding: "When the dust settles it may even be the Hunger Games that holds up best."

Sunrise on the Reaping is set 24 years before the first Hunger Games film, and 40 years after the previous prequel, 2023's The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes.

"This prequel lands at some mid-point between Ballad and Hunger Games, which puts it on an immediately odd footing," Empire said in a three-star review, external.

"It can't escape the sense of feeling supplementary. It's an enjoyable-enough diversion, but essentially a footnote with aspirations."

Screen Daily called it, external an "underwhelming prequel", which "suffers from a lack of compelling characters" and "feels oddly incidental - a drab afterthought rather than a crucial new chapter".

The film's all-star cast includes Ralph Fiennes, Jesse Plemons, Glenn Close, Kieran Culkin, Elle Fanning, Mckenna Grace and Maya Hawke alongside Joseph Zada as the 16-year-old Abernathy.

IndieWire, external said Zada's performance is "charming enough", but "his character lacks the gravitational charisma or arc that, say, Jennifer Lawrence brought to the original films".

The movie feels "a little bit like a cold cash grab rather than a necessary deepening of the series' lore" and is "a dreary slog", IndieWire's critic wrote.

The New York Times, external also used the word "slog", adding: "One really misses the guiding presence of Jennifer Lawrence, who had the raw pathos to both ground and expand a world in a way many younger stars often can't.

"In Sunrise, we're instead left with fleeting moments in which Plemons or Ralph Fiennes (playing the evil President Snow) briefly elevate the film. They seem to be trapped in this dystopia too."

Entertainment.title: James Bond: Robert Pattinson to replace Daniel Craig as 007
Entertainment.text:
Robert Pattinson, the British actor known for films such as Twilight and The Batman, has been confirmed as the next actor to play James Bond.

The announcement was made by Amazon MGM Studios in a social media post on Monday, with a picture showing Pattinson in character as 007.

The 40-year-old becomes the seventh actor to play the famous fictional spy and will star in the 26th Bond movie, due to be released in 2028.

In a statement, the London-born actor said: "James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime."

The next Bond film will be directed by Denis Villeneuve and written by Steven Knight, but its title and exact release date have not yet been announced.

In his statement, Pattinson said he was "deeply grateful" to the film's creative team "for their belief in me".

"To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement," he added. "I couldn't be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team."

The announcement comes after years of intense speculation about who will take over from Daniel Craig in one of the most high-profile - and highly scrutinised - roles in entertainment.

The next 007 film will be the first since long-term Bond producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G Wilson stepped back and Amazon took creative control of the franchise, after acquiring the series' parent company MGM.

By the time the 26th Bond film is released, it will have been seven years since the last - 2021's No Time To Die - the biggest gap in the franchise's history.

Director Villeneuve is best known for films including the Dune trilogy, Prisoners, Sicario, Arrival and Blade Runner 2049, while writer Knight is known for TV hits Peaky Blinders and House of Guinness, and films including Burnt, Spencer and Locke.

Pattinson has already worked with Villeneuve on Dune: Part 3, where he stars as a new villain, Scytale. The film is released next month.

In a statement reacting to Pattinson's Bond casting, Villeneuve said: "Before anything else, I want to express my deep gratitude to the remarkable actors who joined us on this journey.

"We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007. I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond.

"He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin."

Pattinson's casting was also welcomed by Buckingham Palace, with a post on Instagram sharing the news and adding: "Welcome to His Majesty's Secret Service, Mr Bond."

Australian actor George Lazenby, who played James Bond in the 1969 film On Her Majesty's Secret, posted a video on social media welcoming Pattinson to "the most exclusive club in the world".

"Remember to enjoy yourself... Let's see if you'll have 'this never happened to the other fella' moment," Lazenby said.

"All the best mate."

Several other actors, including Josh O'Connor, Callum Turner and Jack Lowden, were reported to be in the frame for the role as screen tests took place in recent weeks.

But Amazon MGM ultimately went with a household name, choosing a more bankable movie star who is widely seen as a safe pair of hands.

Craig appeared in five Bond movies in total, starting with 2006's Casino Royale, and spent 16 years as the secret agent created by author Ian Fleming.

In a statement, Fleming's estate said they were "delighted to welcome Robert Pattinson to the James Bond family".

The next film will mark a new era for the franchise. Amazon purchased MGM for $8.5bn in 2021, which included the rights to distribute James Bond.

Then in 2025, long-time Bond producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G Wilson agreed to sell creative control of the franchise to Amazon MGM.

Before that, the franchise had been under the Broccoli family's control since 1962's Dr. No, when Sean Connery first starred as Bond.

The Broccoli family preserved the integrity of the character and brand for decades, resisting spin-offs and licensing that some industry experts now expect to see following Amazon's takeover.

Entertainment.title: Woman who accuses Russell Brand of rape says prison message 'upsetting'
Entertainment.text:
A woman who has made allegations against Russell Brand has said she finds it "upsetting" and "really shocking" that he was able to claim he was innocent from prison, following his conviction for rape and sexual assault.

Speaking after the comedian's wife Laura read out a message from him on their Sunday Service show on YouTube, Mia Latter told BBC Radio 4's Today programme she found it "appalling" to hear "this Christian message alongside absolute lies".

"I just felt for those women that stood trial and everything they went through," she said.

Latter, 37, who has alleged she was raped by Brand when she was 16, was not a complainant in his recent criminal trial and he denies her claims.

Brand is currently serving a 10-and-half-year prison sentence after being found guilty at Southwark Crown Court of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, involving four women.

In recent years he has positioned himself as a Christian influencer, and has a large following, including in the US. In the message read out by his wife on their show, Brand said: "I am not guilty of the offences I have been jailed for."

Latter said the broadcast "was really shocking to me... it was appalling, frankly, it was upsetting to watch".

She said the woman who gave evidence in the trial "got their verdict, and for him to say, 'I'm innocent, I'm not guilty' - well, you are, you're a convicted rapist now. There's no arguing with that".

Downing Street said on Monday it expects action to be taken if Brand is found to have broken prison rules.

Justice Secretary Alex Norris said that "prisoners are rightly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims".

Latter said she was 16 when she met Brand, who was 30 at the time.

She was one of six women who made allegations against him as part of a Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches investigation in 2023. None of the women were involved in his recent trial.

In an interview with the Sunday Times this week, Latter said Brand told her to keep their relationship secret from her school friends and claimed that he referred to her as "the child" in front of his entourage.

She has waived her right to anonymity in order to campaign for a staggered age of consent to be introduced in the UK that would make sexual relationships between 16 and 17 year-olds and adults illegal.

Latter told the Sunday Times the Crown Prosecution Service decided not to include her as part of Brand's criminal trial but police wanted her to be part of "subsequent" proceedings. She told the paper that she would not continue with the criminal process so she could focus on her campaign.

Entertainment.title: Danny Robins drama The Witch Farm inspired by Brecon 'ghost story'
Entertainment.text:
The "real-life ghost story" of a family who experienced "frightening, inexplicable" things after moving to the countryside has been turned into a new TV drama.

The Witch Farm tells the "truly nightmarish" tale of Liz and Bill Rich who left London with their son Jonathan for a remote farmhouse in the foothills of the Brecon Beacons, determined to make a fresh start.

At first the isolation felt like freedom, but the family claimed things began to happen around the house leading them to feel increasingly scared.

Writer and creator, Danny Robins, met Liz who told him "her incredible story", becoming a four-part series he believes will "really surprise people".

Robins, who was also the executive producer of the project, explained how the idea for the four-part series came from a podcast he made for the BBC called The Battersea Poltergeist, which he described as being based on "another real-life ghost story".

"It was a hit around the world and afterwards there was a lot of pressure to find a sequel," he said, which led him to discover the story of Liz and Bill Rich.

In 1989, the young couple moved their family into a remote farmhouse at the foot of a mountain. They claimed to have experienced poltergeist activity, apparitions, alleged possessions and even physical injury.

They say this lasted for seven years and changed them forever, as well as affecting the community around them.

Robins said: "The more I dug into it, the more it felt like something that merited a long-form approach and so we made the podcast series called The Witch Farm.

"Through that process, I met Liz and she told me her incredible story. We also found other witnesses and pieced everything together through a mix of audio drama and documentary.

After finishing the podcast, Robins asked himself "what's next?", admitting that telling the story as a TV documentary "didn't feel right", leading to the decision to dramatise it instead.

Asked what he hopes viewers will feel when they watch the series, Robins said: "I absolutely want people to feel scared, but I also want them to be moved by it.

"It's an incredibly powerful and emotional story, that was one of the things that grabbed me when I first came across it for the podcast."

He also hopes that viewers will "laugh a little", adding that "humour has always been important" to his work.

Robins also hopes to raise the question – 'do ghosts exist?', sparking the debate between belief and scepticism.

"What's crucial for me is that I want viewers to think about it and reach their own conclusions," he said.

The upcoming drama, which was filmed in Wales, stars Port Talbot-born actress Gabrielle Creevy.

She said: "I'm from Wales and I love working here. It's always a pleasure and crews are always so great. I love working in the middle of nowhere in the fresh air - I think I'll always feel the same."

Robins said she brought "absolute authenticity to the role" through her Welsh accent."

Creevy recently featured in the new season of spy thriller Black Doves where she also uses her Welsh accent.

Robins said The Witch Farm is "such a Welsh story", which was considered throughout making the production.

He said an "almost entirely Welsh" crew was used in it's creation, adding: "It's been important that this feels like a story made and told in Wales."

The Witch Farm will be available on BBC iPlayer, BBC One and BBC One Wales from Sunday, 22 November.

Entertainment.title: Grammys 2027: Raye leads with 11 nominations as Dolly Parton receives posthumous nods
Entertainment.text:
British singer Raye leads the charge at the forthcoming Grammy Awards with 11 nominations, while Dolly Parton has been recognised with three posthumous nods.

Raye is nominated for her latest Mercury-winning record This Album May Contain Hope and its lead single Where Is My Husband!, which is up for both song and record of the year.

Other nominees include Rosalía, Ella Langley, Olivia Dean, Ariana Grande, Bruno Mars, Taylor Swift, Olivia Rodrigo, Miranda Lambert and Phoebe Bridgers.

Parton's two nominations, both in the best country duo/group performance category, come three months after the country music star died aged 80.

Parton is recognised for Butterfly, her collaboration with the Zac Brown Band, and Light of a Clear Blue Morning, alongside an all-star line-up including her goddaughter Miley Cyrus.

The late country star also received a nomination for best audio book, for her narration of Star of the Show: My Life on Stage.

The Grammy Awards 2027 will take place on Sunday 7 February in Los Angeles.

Madonna's album Confessions II, a sequel to 2005's Confessions on a Dancefloor, was absent from the "big four" categories - including album, record and song of the year.

That will be seen by many as the Grammys continuing their tradition of snubbing the US singer, but the album did make it into the best dance category.

Rosalía's nine nominations for her widely acclaimed album Lux come after her huge success at last week's Latin Grammy Awards.

Langley's seven nominations include song of the year for her breakthrough hit Choosin' Texas, which this year became the longest-running number one single in the history of Billboard's Hot 100.

Entertainment.title: 'Look who it isnae' - Still Game set to return as stage show
Entertainment.text:
Seven years ago, Scotland's most beloved pensioners climbed to the top of Ben Lomond and reached the big Clansman in the sky.

But now, Jack Jarvis and Victor McDade have been resurrected as Still Game returns to the stage for a special run of shows.

The stage show, Still Game Live: Heaven Sent, will have a 10-date run at the Ovo Hydro in Glasgow from February 2028.

Creators Ford Kiernan and Greg Hemphill joked they had a "fear of moving on" after announcing the characters' return.

The ninth and final series of the BBC comedy aired in 2019.

However, the last appearance of the duo came in another stage show, Still Game: The Final Farewell, later the same year.

Kiernan and Hemphill previously said the final series and stage show would be the "final nail in the final coffin".

They did adapt the series for a comic book, which was released in 2024.

In a statement, they said: "We had FOMO (Fear of moving on).

"Haud oan! Whit's been happenin? It's been far too lang…Craiglang."

Entertainment.title: Birmingham university pauses Shakespeare Institute move after backlash
Entertainment.text:
The University of Birmingham has paused plans to move the Shakespeare Institute from Stratford-upon-Avon to Birmingham amid growing opposition to the proposal.

The university said it would spend the next six months working with partners including the Royal Shakespeare Company (RSC) and the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust to explore the institute's future in Stratford.

The decision comes after criticism from Stratford-upon-Avon MP Manuela Perteghella and a petition that attracted more than 12,000 signatures.

The move from its home at Mason Croft had been due to take place in September.

The postgraduate research institute announced on Friday that it had been told it would leave Stratford and relocate to the University of Birmingham's Edgbaston campus, with future plans unclear for its Mason Croft base, historic gardens and playing fields.

Announcing the pause on Tuesday evening, University of Birmingham vice-chancellor and principal Prof Adam Tickell said he had heard "very clearly" how much the institute mattered to Stratford-upon-Avon and the wider Shakespeare community.

"I have therefore decided to pause the planned move as we explore how and whether the Institute can have a vibrant and viable future in Stratford-upon-Avon," he said.

Entertainment.title: Emma Barnett: Host to leave Radio 4's Today and start new BBC show
Entertainment.text:
Radio 4 presenter Emma Barnett is set to leave the Today programme this week for a multiplatform new BBC show in the New Year.

Former Woman's Hour host Barnett has developed a "bold" new show, she says, which will launch in 2027 across BBC Sounds, BBC iPlayer and YouTube.

Her final day presenting Radio 4's flagship morning news and current affairs show will be on Wednesday 18 November.

"For the last nearly six years - it's been incredible to talk to the mighty Radio 4 listeners," she said in a statement. "Having proudly hosted Woman's Hour and now the Today Programme - I've had the rare pleasure of hosting nearly every hour of the morning on this truly unique and special radio network."

She added: "But it's not goodbye to the BBC audience I value so greatly because I have something else for them that I hope will add something meaningful and entertaining to their lives."

Posting on Instagram, external, she said there would be more information on what her new show would be about soon.

"Watch this space and look ready. I am… More soon."

Barnett joined Today in May 2024, taking over from Martha Kearney to work alongside fellow presenters Anna Foster, Nick Robinson and Justin Webb, as well as Mishal Husain and Amol Rajan who have also since left.

Today programme editor Rebecca Keating said Barnett had brought "enormous energy" to Today, with "a keen focus" on listeners.

She noted how Barnett had a proven "track record of telling stories of personal hardship that influence public debate" but how she was "also equally at home interviewing British icons like Dame Judi Dench.

"We will miss her generous tea making and wish her every success in her new venture."

In August, Barnett, 41, revealed she had had a hysterectomy and surgery for endometriosis, days before a documentary she made about the condition was broadcast.

She returned to the Today programme explaining she had been absent in recent weeks because she was in hospital "in a case of life imitating work".

Speaking on her BBC podcast, Ready to Talk with Emma Barnett, last year, she told listeners that finding out she was going through perimenopause at the age of 38 felt like she had been "mugged, robbed".

The broadcaster said it was the "first time in my life I haven't really wanted to be a woman - it's the first time I've thought, I'd really quite like to be a bloke".

Radio 4 controller Mohit Bakaya said he was "delighted she's staying with the BBC" and would "look forward to her new show."

BreakingNewsTab.title: Andy Burnham promises to 'move quickly' on Neets report
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The prime minister has said he wants to "move quickly" on implementing recommendations in Alan Milburn's report on work and young people.

Speaking to BBC Breakfast, Andy Burnham said: "This isn't about waiting forever and a long-off-promised reform, I want to get stuck into it right now."

Milburn's report, external urged more job support for under-25s, a shake-up of the benefits system, early intervention in schools and tax cuts for businesses hiring young people.

The government said it backed the review's principles and is expected to set out which proposals it will take on shortly.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said there was no need for "costly government schemes to fix Labour's own mistakes".

"We need to stop making it so expensive and risky to hire young people," she added.

Last year, the government asked Milburn, a former Labour minister, to do a review into the rising number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet), which has now reached almost one million.

Burnham praised the report as a "landmark moment" adding: "This is not just a benefits reform, it's a whole society change he is calling for."

Asked what the number of young people not in education, employment or training should be by the next election, Burnham said he wanted the level to come down "as soon as possible".

He said he wanted 45-day work placements offered to every 16-18-year-old "who wants one" and was working on funding the places.

The government has also announced it will fully fund college places for everyone aged 16 to 18 in England for 2027/28.

The Association of Colleges said the money would allow its members to enrol thousands of extra students each year "confident in the knowledge that they will receive funding for them".

Burnham said he wanted to get the benefit bill down adding: "No one can be comfortable with the idea of hundreds of thousands of young people on benefits - nobody, not me, not anyone."

However, he added that it required "more than the crude cuts the other parties are offering".

"All of my experience says a 'names not numbers' approach that looks at the whole person, their housing, their debt, their mental health issues and creates a rounded response, that is proven to be more successful at getting people into work."

In his report, Milburn warned that employer National Insurance, wage costs, business rates and employment protections could be factors in deterring employers from hiring unexperienced young people.

"Fair pay, greater security and predictable hours matter," Milburn said, but added that the cost and complexity of hiring young people had increased "sharply".

On workers' rights, Burnham argued a balance had to be struck adding: "The more you strengthen employment security that creates more durable jobs that young people are more likely to stay in."

Asked if former Chancellor Rachel Reeves had made the situation worse by increasing the tax employers pay, the prime minister said the government had increased support for those hiring long-term unemployed people.

He also defended his reset with the EU, which could make it easier for young Europeans to work in the UK.

He argued that a closer relationship with the EU would help grow the economy, which would provide more opportunities for young people.

Attempts to change the welfare system under Sir Keir Starmer last year failed when Labour backbenchers refused to support the £5bn cuts to benefits, raising concerns about the impact on disabled people.

So far, there are few signs that Burnham's plans will trigger a similar backlash, although some Labour backbenchers and the Unison trade union have said the proposals on benefits could push young people into poverty.

Steve Darling, the Liberal Democrat work and pensions spokesman, said the government should "scrap the damaging job tax" and work with European countries to grow the economy.

Green Party MP Sian Berry urged the minister to "reject cuts" for young disabled people.

"One million young people need a leg up - one that does not come with the chair being kicked out from under them," she said.

Reform UK said immigration was the "elephant in the room" and called on the government to cut employer national insurance for British workers "so that young Brits are at the front of the queue for new jobs".

BreakingNewsTab.title: Chris Mason: Milburn may have gifted Labour MPs a moral argument for welfare reform
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The prime minister describes Alan Milburn's report on jobs, training and benefits for young people as a "watershed moment".

In so doing, he is accepting Milburn's case for change and taking on the task of delivering it. Were ministers to actually manage that, it would amount to one of the most significant shake-ups of the welfare state in its history.

But the proposed timeframe for this stretches to a decade, which is another geological era in political terms, at least two general elections away.

Milburn is a deft operator. From a round of morning television and radio interviews, to addressing the cabinet, to releasing his report into the wild, he was still out and about on Tuesday evening in Westminster persuading, charming and cajoling those possibly in need of all three.

And this former MP, still every inch the politician, has an ongoing role - appointed the chairman of the government's new Youth Opportunities Unit.

The new job, which will report directly to Andy Burnham, is about tying together the myriad different aspects of change he is suggesting, involving multiple government departments.

And yes, it does mean a 68-year-old bloke becomes an early beneficiary of new employment prospects for the young.

But that glib observation apart, there is a hope that Milburn has gifted Labour MPs a moral argument for welfare reforms they can endorse. Or, to put it more bluntly, one not grounded in a specific objective to make benefits cuts to make the sums add up elsewhere.

Plus, him hanging around perhaps means he can be a useful lightning conductor for any forthcoming angst on Labour's benches – as having persuaded them of the big picture mission, the gritty reality of implementing it begins to take shape.

As the prime minister puts it in an interview in the Times, external, the government wants to offer "a new social contract" for "the let-down generation".

And he tells the newspaper that the initial upfront cost of around £500m, for employment support in 2027-28, will come from existing government budgets, which will mean cuts to other things elsewhere in government.

"I've asked the cabinet to reprioritise," he said.

Crucially, if you are in Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland, many of the decisions around whether or not to press ahead with these ideas will be up to the devolved governments in Edinburgh, Cardiff and Belfast.

From the government at Westminster's perspective, the focus now will be drawing up the specific plans for implementing Milburn's ideas, having accepted the broad thrust of his argument.

A white paper will follow in the new year, and then legislation.

What we don't know yet and will be crucial to the next stage of this debate, is precisely who will be the perceived winners and losers, at least in the short term, of the proposed changes.

Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden told me that "those with the most severe and lifelong disabilities where work is not a realistic prospect" should, as Milburn suggests, "get more support than they receive at the moment". But how will those in this category be defined?

McFadden also told me that for some of those facing "extra costs" associated with their circumstances "there will be an extra cost benefit that will make at least a contribution towards that".

Again, how will those in this category be defined?

There is too an emerging political argument, following remarks from Alan Milburn already seized upon by the Conservatives, that decisions taken by Labour in its first few years in power have made a difficult situation harder still for young people looking for work.

On page 66 of his report, external, Milburn says the Employment Rights Act 2025 "could have major implications at a time when the youth labour market is already weak".

Interestingly, on this point, the prime minister is willing to push back, telling BBC Breakfast that "there is a balance to be struck".

"It is important to consider on the other side of this that the more you strengthen employment security, that can create more durable jobs that young people are more likely to stay in," he says. "We're going to consider all of this in the round."

The big decisions, then, now sit on the prime minister and the work and pensions secretary's desks.

In accepting the magnitude of Milburn's diagnosis and proposed treatment, they are tacitly accepting too that it is their responsibility to deliver – or at least begin to deliver – on much of what he suggests.

Their success or otherwise will matter to this generation of young people and those that will follow – and to the sustainability of the benefits system in the years ahead.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Waymo temporarily pulls driverless taxis from all US freeways
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Waymo has temporarily suspended its driverless vehicles from operating on all US freeways, the company has said.

The decision comes after California banned Waymo's driverless taxis from state freeways following a series of recent traffic incidents.

California's Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) cited an "imminent hazard to public safety" for the ban, noting an incident this month in which several driverless Waymo vehicles entered an active construction zone on US Route 101.

Waymo said it was working with state officials "diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations", adding that no injuries or collisions were reported following the incident on US Route 101 south of San Francisco.

California's DMV said Waymo's driverless taxis presented a risk "due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present".

In another incident earlier this month, footage widely seen on social media appeared to show a Waymo car trying to overtake patrol vehicles that were deliberately slowing the pace of traffic on a San Francisco highway.

The California ban, which came into effect on 11 November, would remain in place until Waymo "demonstrates to the department that it has taken effective corrective actions to address the deficiencies that precipitated the restrictions".

A Waymo spokesperson said: "In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance."

Data on Waymo's website suggests that its cars, compared to human drivers, are involved in 95% fewer crashes resulting in serious injury.

Waymo currently operates driverless taxis in 15 US cities, but only offered freeway rides in a handful of those locations, including San Francisco, Los Angeles and Miami.

The company's driverless taxis can continue to operate on regular city streets.

In May, Waymo recalled thousands of its self-driving cars in the US over a software issue that could allow vehicles to drive into flooded roads.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Irishman charged with destroying US military aircraft with axe
BreakingNewsTab.text:
US officials have charged an Irishman with destroying a $60m (£45m) American military aircraft after he allegedly snuck onto the tarmac of an airport in Ireland.

Daithi O'Corrain, 48, is accused of doing extensive research before he allegedly used chemicals and various tools - including an axe - to damage a US Air National Guard C-130 Hercules parked at Shannon Airport near Limerick.

American prosecutors have charged him with destruction of government property, which carries a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison.

O'Corrain is not currently in US custody, according to the Associated Press news agency, and it is unclear whether he has a lawyer who could speak on his behalf.

In filings unsealed by prosecutors in New York on Tuesday, agents from the FBI argued that the act jeopardised US national security. They say the plane was parked at the airport while en route to another country on a US military assignment.

"As alleged, Daithi O'Corrain carried out a deliberate, planned attack against a US military aircraft, causing tens of millions of dollars in damage and jeopardizing critical military operations," prosecutors said in a court filing.

"This was not an act of spontaneous vandalism," said FBI Assistant Director in Charge James Barnacle Jr, explaining O'Corrain "spent months researching the aircraft, acquiring tools and materials, and preparing to maximize the destruction he could inflict."

Officials say that the suspect planned extensively for the 11 April 2026 raid, and brought tools with him for the demolition, which took place over several hours.

He entered the plane by breaking a locking mechanism, officials say, then used straps to close the doors before covering the windows.

"O'Corrain then proceeded to inflict severe damage to the interior of the Aircraft by, among other things, cutting wire bundles and hydraulic lines within the Aircraft, crimping a liquid oxygen line within the Aircraft, destroying every gauge in the Aircraft's cockpit, and puncturing the Aircraft's air ducts," the US indictment says.

He also used gallium, a substance that can erode aluminum and steel, ball bearings which he poured in the fuel tank, and an axe which he used to puncture the exterior of the plane.

He was caught by airport crew, and filmed standing on top of the plane. He was arrested at the scene, and charged by Ireland's national police with causing criminal damages.

BreakingNewsTab.title: American soldier arrested in UK taken into US military custody
BreakingNewsTab.text:
A US Army officer arrested in the UK on suspicion of spying for Russia earlier this month has been taken into US military custody, British counter-terror police havesaid.

The serviceman has been identified as Lt Col Brandon Carroll Tyner, BBC News understands. The 41-year-old - who served in the US Army since 2008 - was arrested near Gloucester last week by British counter-terror police.

Tyner was based at Imjin Barracks in Innsworth, Gloucestershire, the headquarters of Nato's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps.

Counter Terrorism Policing said he is now in US custody over suspected national security and espionage allegations. At the time of his arrest, Russia said it had "nothing to do with it".

British police previously said he was being held in London after he was arrested under section one and section three of the National Security Act 2023, which relate to obtaining or disclosing protected information, and assisting a foreign intelligence service.

The day after Tyner's arrest on 10 November, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he was "unaware" of what it was connected to.

"We have nothing to do with it, and it has nothing to do with us," he told reporters in Moscow.

On Tuesday, Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing, said: "Subsequently, a decision was made to pass the investigation to them [their American partners] to progress."

"These are extremely serious allegations, and our collective response should send a strong message that we will act swiftly and robustly where we suspect this kind of espionage activity taking place," he added.

Tyner's arrest was the result of a long-running operation by MI5 - the UK's domestic intelligence and security agency - in collaboration with the FBI, the BBC understands.

He had previously served in Afghanistan and Iraq, but at the time of his arrest was working with NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps near Gloucester - where he was said to be entrusted with sensitive information which would have been extremely damaging if leaked to Russia.

Detectives sent the Crown Prosecution Service a file on the senior US soldier's alleged spying for consideration - allegations described by the head of Counter Terrorism Policing as "extremely serious."

But at that stage the Attorney General's Office in London got involved. As did the US authorities.

And now the decision has been taken that Lieutenant Colonel Tyner should be taken into custody by the US Military.

It means he will not stand trial in the UK, but under US Uniform Code of Military Justice.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Philippines police ask prosecutors to charge Thomas Markle over child sex abuse material
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Police in the Philippines have asked prosecutors to charge Thomas Markle Sr, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, with possession of and intent to distribute child sexual abuse material.

Cebu province prosecutor Graeme Elmido told the BBC that police had filed documents requesting that Markle be charged on Monday.

Earlier this month, Markle, 82, was separately arrested and charged in the US with possession of child sexual abuse material. The FBI said agents seized about 78 items, including film negatives, slides and books that they allege contained child sex abuse material, from storage units Markle rented.

Markle, who is in custody in the US, has previously denied the allegations. The BBC has contacted Markle's attorney for comment.

Elmido told the BBC that Philippine National Police had asked prosecutors to charge Markle with "two counts of intent to distribute CSAEM [child sexual abuse and exploitation material], and one count of possession of CSAEM material".

Last month, police in the Philippines obtained a warrant to examine devices allegedly removed from Markle's former home in the country.

Four boxes of material, including computers, phones, hard drives and old video tapes, were handed to officers by Meghan's half brother Thomas Markle Jr.

Earlier this month, Markle Sr was arrested and charged in the US. He had initially been placed under house detention at his assisted living facility in Florida, but was taken back into custody last week after prosecutors alleged he removed his ankle monitor.

Meghan Markle has been estranged from her father since 2018. The BBC understands she broke contact with him last year, telling him she and the authorities knew he had abused young girls.

In a previously shared statement after the allegations against her father emerged, Meghan wrote: "I am deeply distressed... my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed."

She said she hoped it could be understood why she had largely cut off contact from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children".

BreakingNewsTab.title: Home secretary plans to tackle 'perception of two-tier policing'
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood is to announce stronger guidance on police impartiality to tackle what she calls the "corrosive and growing perception of two-tier policing".

She will tell a conference of police chiefs that they should avoid what she calls "misguided attempts at course correction" where the pursuit of equality leads instead to differential treatment.

Recent complaints about alleged two-tier policing have mostly come from those on the right in politics.

They have pointed to the arrest of Henry Nowak as he was dying after being stabbed by Vickrum Digwa who had accused him of racism.

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has argued that white people are treated differently by police because of their race. But critics say this claim risks overlooking the long‑standing experiences of black and minority ethnic communities.

Some senior police figures have also strongly rejected the claim of two-tier policing.

Mahmood will announce a new national standard is being developed "to ensure all members of the public are treated equally", said the Home Office.

"Now let me be clear: I know the vast majority of officers police impartially and that policing without fear or favour is their creed," she will say.

But Mahmood will announce "clear, comprehensive guidance" on police impartiality, which reinforces that officers must apply the law consistently to avoid what she called "motivated actors" whipping up the idea that there's two-tier policing.

Mahmood will say that community engagement can mean going to a residents' association meeting and having tea and biscuits - or samosas - but it shouldn't mean engaging with activists pushing an agenda.

"Leave the politics to the politicians," she will say. "And we will leave the policing to you."

The home secretary will add that more needs to be done to tackle inequalities in policing, highlighting the persistently low proportion of black police officers.

However, she will state that some "well-intentioned approaches", such as the Police Anti-Racism Commitment, "have risked undermining confidence in impartial policing".

"As a Muslim home secretary, no one can doubt that equality in policing, and in our forces, matters to me," she will say.

"But we must also be wary of misguided attempts at course correction, where the pursuit of equality leads instead to differential treatment.

"To the public, it was patently absurd to tell police officers that fair policing "does not mean treating everyone the same".

Jo Noakes who leads the College of Policing, the standards-setting body for the police, said it will issue new guidance for officers that will make clear on impartiality in Spring.

She said: "Policing must act in a way that maintains public confidence, which is dependent on officers and staff exercising their powers without fear or favour...

"Impartiality cannot be seen in isolation but needs to be considered alongside how policing acts with fairness and inclusion - both in its own ranks and with the public."

BreakingNewsTab.title: Cutting EV target risks UK missing climate targets, warns adviser
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The UK is likely to miss legally binding climate targets if the government reduces electric vehicle (EV) targets, independent adviser the Climate Change Committee (CCC) has warned.

In a letter to Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander, the CCC argues that weakening the targets would result in "economic and energy security costs" and leave households "more exposed to volatile fossil fuel prices".

The CCC says that switching to an electric vehicle can save a typical household around £800 a year, with fewer people benefiting if the targets were watered down.

The warning comes after weeks of speculation that the government plans to announce changes to the EV targets. Government sources insist no decision has been made.

Under the current rules, a "zero emission vehicle" (ZEV) mandate requires 80% of new cars sold in the UK to be zero emission by 2030 and all new cars to meet that standard by 2035. Companies that fail to meet their ZEV mandate face a potential fine of £12,000 per car, although there are exemptions.

Industry groups have long complained the current rules impose too heavy a burden, calling instead for a "sustainable transition".

Latest data from trade body the Society of Motor Manufacturing and Traders (SMMT) shows that EVs, as well as plug-in hybrids, are driving growth in new car sales.

In the year so far, 26.6% of all new car registrations have been fully electric, the SMMT says, which is below the headline target of 33% for 2026.

But the industry as a whole appears on course to comply with this year's mandate once flexibilities are accounted for, according to analysis by New AutoMotive, a transport research organisation which supports the transition to electric cars

SMMT Chief Executive Mike Hawes accused the CCC of ignoring the costs of the targets it was defending.

"The industry cannot subsidise the transition indefinitely, which is why it is unified in seeking change," he said.
